Global caveats

Issue Reading note
Segment margins are transfer-price constructs Intel Foundry's revenue is 98.3% intersegment ($17,519M of $17,826M in FY2025), booked at prices "intended to approximate market pricing." CCG's 28.9% and DCAI's 20.2% FY2025 operating margins are struck after paying that internal price; Intel Foundry's −57.9% is not an external-market loss. The two numbers that are real are $12,739M of Intel Products operating income and a $2,214M consolidated operating loss. Every segment margin in this document should be read with that caveat attached.
No continuous segment history Intel recast its segments four times in ten years. The current basis (CCG / DCAI / Intel Foundry / All Other) exists only for FY2023–FY2025 annually and FY2024Q1 onward quarterly. A ten-year segment series cannot be built and is not attempted here.
The latest quarter is eleven weeks old, and the stock moved on an unresolved claim Q1 2026 is the anchor; Q2 2026 prints 2026-07-23. Intel rose roughly 270% in H1 2026, then declined about 21% in the week to 2026-07-09 on press reporting about Intel 18A yields, and sits 22.1% below its June high. The $109.84 price anchor is inside that unresolved drawdown.
Consensus basis is mixed and internally inconsistent Two Bloomberg pulls on the same day give FY2026 revenue consensus of $58,528M (calendar-year override) and $62,366M (BEst fiscal override) — $3,838M apart. Bloomberg's gross-margin and capex consensus series are neither cleanly GAAP nor cleanly non-GAAP. Where consensus appears below, the band is quoted.

Three structural disclosure limits bear on the whole document. Intel maintains no segment balance sheets, allocates no depreciation to the product segments ("impracticable to determine"), and discloses no segment assets, so no segment ROIC or segment EBITDA exists for any Intel segment in any year. Intel has never disclosed an absolute CPU unit count in any period, only percentage changes in volume and ASP, so every unit and ASP level below is a triangulated estimate with bounds. And the FY2025 10-K withdrew segment gross-margin disclosure, which the FY2024 10-K provided, in the year client and server unit costs rose.

1. Business description, model & unit economics

Gap flagged at the top of this section, per §20: "All Other" — Mobileye (80%-owned, separately listed) plus IMS Nanofabrication (68%-owned) — is 6.4% of FY2025 revenue and is covered here only as accounting. Mobileye's unit volumes, design-win pipeline and competitive position against NVIDIA DRIVE and Qualcomm Snapdragon Ride are not analyzed, and nothing below establishes whether the $6.6bn of remaining Mobileye carrying value is at further risk after the Q1 2026 impairment.

Intel designs and manufactures x86 central processing units. It sells them to three PC makers who are 43% of its revenue, to hyperscalers and server builders, and — nominally — it sells manufacturing capacity to outside chip companies, though in practice it has almost none of that business. It reports three segments plus a residual.

(Source: FY2025 10-K, Note 3.)

What sets price: almost nothing durable. For a decade every disclosed ASP move in client was explained by mix, not by list price: notebook ASPs rose 15% in FY2022 on a richer commercial mix and declined 5% in FY2023 on a heavier education mix. In FY2025 client ASPs were "roughly flat" and server ASPs declined 4%, which the 10-K attributes to "pricing actions taken primarily during the first half of 2025 and a higher mix of lower core count products, both driven by a competitive environment." Then, in Q1 2026, Intel raised price for the first time in years: client ASPs rose 16% year over year and server ASPs rose 27%, which the 10-Q attributes to "a higher mix of premium products sold in Q1 2026 and demand-based pricing actions in part to offset higher input costs," with "market demand exceeding supply." That is price taken under scarcity and partly to recover cost, not price taken from a product advantage, and the distinction matters for whether it persists.▪

What sets volume: since Q4 2025, Intel's own fab output. The FY2025 10-K states client volume declined in Q4 2025 "as market demand exceeded our available supply of products due to Intel Foundry wafer fabrication supply constraints, primarily with respect to our Intel 7 process node." Asked on the Q1 2026 call how much revenue Intel was leaving on the table, CFO David Zinsner said only "let's just say it starts with a B" — at least $1bn a quarter, or 7%-plus of the quarter's $13,577M. The binding constraint on Intel's revenue is now a process node that entered high-volume manufacturing in 2017, and Intel is adding wafer starts to it in 2026.▪

What sets cost: depreciation, and a node transition that runs the wrong way. Intel's cost of sales as a percentage of revenue went from 44.6% in FY2021 to 65.2% in FY2025 while depreciation went from 12.6% of revenue to 20.4% — depreciation alone explains roughly 38% of the gross-margin collapse since FY2021.▪ Normally a new node lowers unit cost. Intel's raised it: the FY2025 10-K cites "higher client unit costs resulting from an increased mix of newer generation products sold in 2025," and the CFO says Panther Lake's gross margin is "still below the corporate average" while Intel 18A is "a pretty decent headwind to our gross margins." The new parts are multi-tile, Foveros-packaged, and partly built by TSMC, which is structurally more expensive than the fully-depreciated monolithic Intel 7 part they replace.▪

The demand-driver tree — Intel's revenue reduces to two eroding x86 unit-share positions (PC and server CPUs) monetized at a price set, since Q4 2025, by Intel's own wafer shortage, not by product advantage; the AI-compute dollar the framing leans on ("AI PC," "AI-driven businesses now 60% of revenue," the "approaching $1 trillion" semi TAM, "process leadership regained") accrues to NVIDIA and to TSMC, not to Intel. The crux is that every driver management points to as forward growth resolves, in the realized numbers, into share Intel is losing, price taken under scarcity, or a foundry customer that does not yet exist.

Demand driver Share of revenue Ultimate exposure (decomposed) Realized 3-yr contribution Robustness

Reduces to Intel's revenue capture per PC shipped, which fell $107.5 → $97.0 (2023→2025, −11.3%, §6). "AI PC" is a mix label inside this, not a unit lever. Client revenue flat over the three disclosed segment years (CCG $32,305M → $32,228M, FY2023→FY2025); across the FY2021 peak CCG is ~$10.8bn of the $19.9bn organic decline (§6). No AI-PC volume uplift appeared: client revenue fell $28.7bn → $27.6bn as AI PCs passed 60% of mix. The only 2026 "growth" is +16% ASP under scarcity, which produced negative incremental gross profit (§1a, §8 V2). Structural share erosion on a cyclical, plateauing TAM; the ASP spike is cyclical cost-recovery, not durable. High downside amplitude to the 2026 memory-driven PC downturn (§6).

The AI wave does not land here: the host CPU costs a few thousand dollars against a tens-of-thousands accelerator, so even at 1:1 CPU:GPU attach Intel keeps a single-digit share of the AI compute dollar (§6). Reduces to a shrinking share of the merchant host-CPU pool plus an unverified attach bet that governs units, not dollars. DCAI was the only segment to grow FY2023→FY2025 (+$939M), but FY2024→FY2025 was all volume with ~zero incremental profit and FY2025→Q1'26 was all price (−5% units, +27% ASP, §1b). Across the FY2021 peak DCAI is ~$9.9bn of the organic decline; old DCG's 49.9% FY2018 margin is gone (§13.1). Structural share loss (secular) to AMD and ARM; the recent gain is cycle (x86 server units +10%) plus scarcity price, not trend. High amplitude: AMD's DC revenue ($5,775M) already overtook all of DCAI ($5,052M) in Q1'26 (§8 V6).
Custom ASIC + other DCAI (networking, IPU) ~5% ($2,871M) A custom-silicon / DPU design-win business (~$1bn run-rate) largely fabbed at external foundries, competing with Broadcom (~$20bn AI revenue) and Marvell; the cited "$100bn TAM" is unsourced (§1b). Reduces to Intel's share of merchant custom-ASIC sockets, not to Intel's own fabs. The one genuine growth franchise: grew >50% in 2025 and roughly doubled y/y in Q1'26, but off a base near zero and still ~2% of revenue (§1b, §6). Real, immaterial to the top line, and its wafer economics leak to TSMC. Secular/structural growth, tiny amplitude; does not move consolidated revenue at current scale.
AI accelerator (GPU / Gaudi) ~0% The AI training/inference compute dollar (the largest secular driver in semis) accrues to NVIDIA ($193,700M of DC revenue) and to TSMC as fab, not to Intel. Gaudi was discontinued as "unsuccessful" ($1,297M of inventory charges) and the 10-K concedes Intel "missed the significant shift... to GPUs" (§2, §6). Nets to ~0, and negative after write-offs. The "AI-driven businesses now 60% of revenue, grew 40%" metric is management-defined and reconciles to no segment (CCG +1%, DCAI +22%, Foundry +16% y/y; §13.3). The biggest claimed driver is invisible in Intel's dollars. Not a lever Intel holds; the exposure is a hole, not a driver.
Intel Foundry external / 14A bet 0.6% ($307M external; $17,519M intersegment eliminates) Reduces to (a) ~$0.3bn of trailing external revenue, most of it Altera (a 49%-owned related party) and U.S.-government work (arm's-length competitive external revenue is ~$28M/qtr, ~0.07% of the merchant foundry market, §8 V3); plus (b) a binary bet on a named significant 14A customer, which the 10-K calls "uncertain" and which resolves in 2H 2026 (§7 #4). Advanced packaging (EMIB) is the one credible external path, "billions/yr" per the CFO but unsized, with no revenue before 2027 (§2). Went the wrong way: external revenue $547M (FY2023) → $307M (FY2025) → $174M (Q1'26, down from $222M) (§2). Five years and $100bn-plus of net PP&E produced no significant external customer by Intel's own admission. Contribution to realized growth: negative. Levered to the strongest secular trend in semis and has captured ~0.17% of it; a cost, not a driver, until a 14A customer appears (§6). Binary, not incremental.
Adjacencies & residual (Wi-Fi/Thunderbolt/Arc/edge; Mobileye, IMS) ~15% ($4,600M + $3,563M) Connectivity and edge silicon attached to the same PC/server units above (so it re-exposes to the two CPU drivers), plus Mobileye (80%-owned ADAS, vs NVIDIA DRIVE / Qualcomm) and IMS, neither analyzed as a demand driver; Mobileye took a $3.9bn goodwill impairment in Q1'26 (§13.2). All Other fell $5,463M → $3,563M FY2023→FY2025, mostly the Altera deconsolidation with NAND already exited (§1). Static-to-declining residual with no independent growth driver. Cyclical and derivative of the core CPU volumes; Mobileye a separate, impaired ADAS bet.

Across the three disclosed segment years (FY2023→FY2025) consolidated revenue fell 2.5%, and the only line that grew organically was DCAI's +$939M, itself volume-with-no-profit and then price-under-scarcity. The claimed growth drivers do not appear in the realized dollars: the PC and server "recovery" is cycle plus scarcity price on an eroding x86 unit-share base, the AI compute dollar is captured by NVIDIA and TSMC, and "foundry leadership regained" is a $0.3bn external line going backwards behind a 14A customer that does not yet exist.

1a. Client Computing Group — unit economics

Intel discloses no absolute unit count. The estimate below is triangulated from the PC unit TAM times Mercury Research's x86 share, from AMD's disclosed client units and ASP changes back-solved, and from management's own stated client TAM. The three angles land in a 183–189M band, but they are not fully independent — all three apply Mercury's roughly 74/26 Intel/AMD split, and the AMD back-solve reduces to a single identity (units +31% × ASP +15% = revenue +51%), so it corroborates AMD's internal consistency, not Intel's unit base.

The table closes exactly: client COGS of ~$14,229M plus other-CCG COGS of ~$3,220M equals the $17,451M implied by the segment's combined cost line less opex, and gross profit less opex reproduces the reported $9,317M to the dollar.

The bottom-up cost stack explains the margin. Roughly half of CCG's FY2025 product revenue came from Intel Core parts on Intel 7 — a monolithic die of about 150mm², roughly 395 good die per wafer at a node in volume since 2017, so about $35–40 of manufacturing cost per unit. The other half is Core Ultra: four tiles, with compute and GPU tiles on TSMC N3/N5, Foveros 3D packaging instead of a conventional substrate, and on-package LPDDR5 memory in the Lunar Lake variant — roughly $90–130 per unit [estimate]. Blended at a 50/50 revenue split that is about $74, against the $77 the top-down residual implies.

Management presents only the first of two facts about CCG's Q1 2026. CCG operating income rose $155M year over year to $2,516M. But the 10-Q discloses that operating expense was $249M favorable, so the change in cost of sales was +$192M against a change in revenue of +$98M: CCG's gross profit declined by roughly $94M in the quarter Intel raised client prices 16%.▪ All of the operating-income improvement, and more, came from headcount reduction.

The single most useful number in DCAI is the difference between volume-led and price-led growth, and Intel's own bridges give it. FY2024→FY2025 added $794M of revenue, all of it volume (+9% units, −4% ASP), and produced approximately zero incremental product profit — the 10-K says the benefit of higher revenue "was substantially offset by higher server unit costs from an increased mix of newer generation products." Q1 2025→Q1 2026 added $926M of revenue, all of it price (+27% ASP, −5% units), and the 10-Q attributes $604M of favorable product profit to it: an incremental product margin of roughly 65%. A dollar of volume in DCAI is worth almost nothing; a dollar of price is worth about 65 cents.▪

That asymmetry explains a decision Intel does not spell out. On its disclosed ASPs and estimated die sizes, a Xeon generates roughly $1.45 of revenue per mm² of net silicon against roughly $0.81 for a client CPU — about 1.8x [estimate: blended Xeon ASP ~$1,012 on ~700mm² vs client ASP ~$145 on ~180mm²; both die-size inputs are estimates and the ratio is sensitive to them]. Under a binding wafer constraint the correct allocation rule is gross profit per wafer, and the CFO said on the Q4 2025 call: "Where possible, we're prioritizing our internal wafer supply to data center and leveraging an increased mix of externally sourced wafers in clients." The consequence is visible: in Q1 2026 client volume declined 13% year over year while server volume declined only 5%.

The custom-ASIC line inside "other DCAI" is the one new franchise. It grew more than 50% in 2025, 26% sequentially in Q4 2025, reached an annualized run-rate above $1bn, and in Q1 2026 grew more than 30% sequentially and nearly doubled year over year.▪ The 10-K states IPUs are "manufactured at an external foundry"; whether the whole custom-ASIC line is externally fabricated is not disclosed. Management's "$100 billion TAM" for it is unsourced and undefined — Broadcom, the incumbent that owns this market, did roughly $20bn of AI revenue in its last fiscal year.

1c. Intel Foundry — unit economics

Intel Foundry is not yet a foundry business. It is Intel's manufacturing cost centre with a revenue line attached.▪ Its price is a transfer price benchmarked to what a merchant foundry would charge, its volume is set by Intel Products' demand, and its cost was fixed by capital decisions taken years ago.

Intel Foundry (FY2025) Value TSMC (FY2025) Basis

Revenue $17,826M (of which $307M external) $122,000M 10-K Note 3; TSMC FY2025 results [web]
Revenue per wafer ~$14,900 (incl. back-end and packaging) $8,133 derived
Operating cost per wafer ~$23,500 (range $20,100–28,100) $4,002 derived
Operating profit per wafer ~−$8,600 +$4,132 derived
Operating margin (57.9)% +50.8% 10-K; TSMC [web]

Reconciliation 1.2M × (−$8,600) ≈ −$10.3bn = reported −$10,318M 15.0M × $4,132 ≈ $62bn ≈ 50.8% × $122bn —

The per-wafer rows depend on a wafer-count estimate with wide bounds. The comparison that depends on no estimate at all is the one that matters. Because Intel Foundry's revenue is struck at approximate market prices, its revenue and TSMC's are on a comparable "market value of silicon produced" basis:

Cost per $1.00 of market-priced output Operating margin
Intel Foundry $1.58 (57.9)%
TSMC $0.49 +50.8%

Intel spends 3.2x what TSMC spends to produce a dollar of market-valued silicon.▪ To earn TSMC's operating margin on FY2025 output Intel Foundry would have to cut its $28,144M cost base to $8,770M, a 69% reduction. Caveats narrow this: Intel Foundry absorbs all leading-edge process R&D and all back-end assembly, test and packaging, which TSMC either spends less on or outsources; TSMC's revenue base is 6.8x larger, so fixed-cost absorption alone explains part of the gap; and Intel's node mix is weighted to a trailing node whose market price is discounted. On a mix-adjusted per-wafer basis the manufacturing-cost gap is nearer 2x than 3.2x [estimate].

Why the transfer price is the whole model: intersegment sales are recorded "at prices that are intended to approximate market pricing," so TSMC's price list effectively sets Intel Foundry's revenue. The CFO stated the loss mechanism plainly in Q2 2024: operating losses would continue "with more than 85% of wafer volumes still coming from pre-EUV nodes with an uncompetitive cost structure and power performance and area deficits reflected in market-based [pricing]." Because Intel 7 is power-, performance- and area-deficient against the alternative, the market-based price it earns is discounted; Intel's cost to make it reflects a capital base built for a leadership node at leadership volumes. Low price, high cost, on roughly 85–90% of the volume.

Intel published the design of this model at its June 2023 webinar: the foundry was meant to charge Products cost plus a roughly 10% markup, earn a small positive gross margin, and run a −18% operating margin by construction because it absorbs technology-development R&D [deck: Internal Foundry Model webinar, 2023-06-21, slide 12]. FY2022 came close (−18.8% actual against −18% designed). It broke afterwards: the transfer price now covers about 74% of Intel Foundry's cost of sales, against the 110% the model contemplated.

Break-even: holding the transfer price and cost structure constant and treating depreciation plus segment opex plus a share of fab overhead as fixed, Intel Foundry needs roughly $30–36bn of revenue to break even at the operating line, 1.7x to 2.0x FY2025▪ [estimate: depreciation ~$8,800M + segment opex ~$4,155M fixed; non-depreciation COGS split fixed/variable across a 40–70% band]. That band should not be treated as a target, because the cost base it is computed against is not static: $34,543M of construction in progress is not yet depreciating (FY2025 10-K, Note 6), which at Intel's 8-year machinery life adds roughly $4.3bn a year of depreciation as it enters service. Consolidated depreciation already rose 37.1% over two years ($7,847M to $10,757M) while Intel Foundry's revenue declined 3.7%. Internal demand cannot close the gap either: Intel Foundry's intersegment revenue runs at roughly 36% of Intel Products revenue, so even 20% growth at Intel Products adds only about $3.5bn.

The one part of the model with customer pull is advanced packaging, and it is not in the P&L. It is discussed in §2 and §5.

2. Key technologies & technical differentiators

Intel has real technology. It does not currently have technical differentiation in the place investors are looking. The leading-edge node — Intel 18A, with RibbonFET and PowerVia — is a real engineering achievement that arrived roughly a year late and is still a gross-margin headwind. The technology where Intel is differentiated, has external design interest, and prices at a premium is advanced packaging, a 2017-vintage capability that does not require Intel to win the node race at all.▪

Technology Status (Q1 2026) Differentiated? Evidence

Intel 4 / Intel 3 HVM 2023 / 2024 No Each "a modest portion" of FY2025 production
Intel 18A (RibbonFET + PowerVia) HVM late 2025 Partly — performance yes, cost no Two industry firsts in volume; still below corporate-average gross margin

EMIB / EMIB-T / Foveros EMIB in HVM since 2017; EMIB-T scaling 2026 Yes The only Intel technology with disclosed external demand "in the billions of dollars per year"
x86 architecture and ecosystem Mature Yes, but eroding Four decades of software; AMD and ARM taking share every quarter
Disaggregated chiplet/tile design All Core Ultra and server CPUs No — it is a dependency Key tiles made by TSMC; "we have no long-term contract with TSMC"

What Intel 18A does: two changes shipped together, both firsts in high-volume manufacturing. RibbonFET is Intel's gate-all-around transistor: the gate wraps the channel on all four sides instead of three, so the same drive current comes from less silicon area and drive current is tuned by ribbon width, not by adding discrete fins. PowerVia moves the power rails to the back of the wafer, leaving the front side for signal routing only, which lowers IR droop and lets signals route more densely — at the cost of a harder process flow, because the wafer must be thinned and bonded. TSMC does not ship backside power on N2; it arrives with A16. On that one axis Intel is ahead of TSMC by about a generation.▪

The published density comparison is more mixed than either side's marketing suggests. On the densest published SRAM bit cell the two are reported as tied: IEEE Spectrum reports both companies' most densely packed SRAM block at 38.1 megabits per square millimetre using a 0.021µm² cell (spectrum.ieee.org, accessed 2026-07-11) [web]. On high-density standard-cell logic density, trade reporting puts Intel 18A at 238 MTr/mm² against TSMC N2's 313 MTr/mm², roughly 24% behind (tomshardware.com, accessed 2026-07-11) [web]. Density sets cost per transistor, which is the first question a fabless foundry customer asks; performance sets price. Intel has traded toward performance, which suits its own high-ASP CPUs and suits a merchant foundry less well.▪

The first 18A product does not win on the metrics a premium notebook buyer compares. Panther Lake (Core Ultra Series 3) scores roughly 2,900–3,000 on Geekbench single-core against 4,070 for Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme and above 4,200 for Apple's M5; its NPU score of about 55,000–56,000 trails Snapdragon's 88,615 (tomsguide.com, accessed 2026-07-11) [web]. It leads on gaming and on x86 compatibility. That is a real but narrow win, and it is the win x86 has always had.

And 18A costs Intel money on every wafer today. The FY2025 10-K booked $878M of higher inventory reserves "primarily related to lower of cost or net realizable value charges for products manufactured on the early ramp of our Intel 18A process node." The Q1 2026 10-Q attributes $489M of Intel Foundry's unfavorable product profit to "an increased mix of higher cost wafers manufactured on our Intel 18A process node." The CFO says foundry-average gross margin is "multiple, multiple quarters" away.▪ Yields are disclosed only as adjectives — "below what I want them to be" in January 2026, "running ahead of the internal projections" in April 2026 — with no absolute number ever given, which makes "ahead of plan" unfalsifiable.

Roadmap execution is the decision-relevant fact, because every element of the bull case is an unshipped product. Of seven dated technology commitments Intel has made in the last six years — 7nm on schedule, five nodes in four years, Intel 20A, process parity in 2024 and leadership in 2025, 18A manufacturing readiness in 2H 2024, the first 18A SKU by end-2025, and the Ohio fab — one was met on the stated terms, and it was the smallest (a single SKU by a quarter-end).▪ Intel 20A was cancelled outright. The 10-K concedes the pattern: "These delays have allowed competitors using third-party foundries, such as TSMC, to benefit from advancements in manufacturing processes introduced ahead of us." Management is now asking for credit on 14A, 18A-P, EMIB-T, Foveros-B/-R, Crescent Island, Jaguar Shores, Diamond Rapids and Coral Rapids — every one of which lands in 2027 or 2028.

Advanced packaging is where the evidence actually is. EMIB embeds a small silicon bridge in the organic package substrate to connect two die at high density. The alternative, TSMC's CoWoS, puts the whole die complex on a large silicon interposer. EMIB uses silicon only where the connection is, so it is not reticle-limited the way an interposer is and it does not consume a full silicon wafer per package. It has been in high-volume manufacturing since 2017 — this is the one place Intel's 2010s R&D compounds into a 2026 asset. EMIB-T, introduced in 2025 and scaling from 2026, adds through-silicon vias for the power delivery and bandwidth that HBM needs. The commercial evidence follows: the CFO said on the Q1 2026 call that he had expected these opportunities "in the hundreds of millions of dollars level" but that demand "is more in the billions of dollars per year kind of level," that "advanced packaging really is a differentiated offering for us," and that "we get very attractive pricing relative to some of the other areas of the foundry business." Intel added to its advanced-packaging backlog in Q1 2026 and announced a multi-year expansion of its Malaysia back-end to support committed demand converting to revenue from 2027. Nothing is in the P&L yet, no dollar figure or customer name has been disclosed, and Intel has already begun outsourcing some EMIB production to Amkor (techpowerup.com, accessed 2026-07-11) [web], which argues against packaging being a scarce Intel-only capability.

The leading-edge node's external traction is the opposite. Intel Foundry external revenue: $547M (FY2023), $159M (FY2024), $307M (FY2025), $174M (Q1 2026). The FY2025 10-K states verbatim: "We have been unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of our nodes and our prospects for securing a significant external foundry customer for Intel 14A are uncertain." After five years and more than $100bn of net PP&E, the leading-edge wafer business has no significant external customer by the company's own admission, while the packaging business nobody models has demand management sizes in the billions per year.▪

The 14A gate moved, quietly, ten weeks after the 10-K. The FY2025 10-K conditions leading-edge continuation on Intel's ability to "secure a significant external customer" for 14A. The Q1 2026 10-Q rewrites the same passage as securing "sufficient committed demand for Intel 14A through product design wins with potential significant external customers and our Intel products roadmap," and adds that "our Intel products roadmap now includes a number of future products that are being designed to utilize Intel 14A." The CEO said on the Q1 2026 call that Intel has "land[ed] more of our own future product tiles on Intel 14A." Intel can now satisfy the condition with its own demand. Whether that is de-risking or a lowered bar is not determinable from the disclosure, but the disclosure moved.

The software layer was announced and then removed. Intel's answer to CUDA was oneAPI plus OpenVINO. Across the FY2020 to FY2025 10-Ks, oneAPI mentions went 7, 7, 8, 6, 3, 1, and OpenVINO went 5, 4, 5, 3, 2, 0. What replaced them, in the FY2025 10-K: "We provide support for AI frameworks such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face, vLLM, and WebNN." That is a backend target for other people's frameworks, whose default backend is CUDA. The same filing still asserts "Our software portfolio is a key differentiator for our DCAI business," which is a differentiator stripped of every named product. The risk factors say the rest: Intel "missed the significant shift in compute demand to GPUs optimized for AI workloads and [has] been unsuccessful to date in becoming a meaningful participant in that market."

3. Competitive advantages & moat assessment

CCG's and DCAI's margins are struck after an internal transfer price, Intel Foundry lost $10,318M on the other side of it, and the allocation is banded at 50–70% below. What Intel Products would report buying wafers at TSMC merchant prices is unknown, so the peer margin gaps below are not fully like-for-like and the moat conclusion carries that limitation (§20).

Intel no longer has a durable competitive advantage in any of its three businesses. What it has is a large, decaying incumbency in x86, an unproven option in advanced packaging, and a manufacturing asset base that has been a cost, not a moat for five years running.▪ Returns are the plainest evidence: Intel's ROIC went from 21.6% in FY2018 to −1.3% in FY2025, below any plausible cost of capital every year since FY2021, while invested capital rose 82% over the decade and NOPAT went from $10,375M to −$1,749M. Every incremental dollar of capital Intel has invested since FY2018 has produced negative incremental NOPAT: rolling three-year ROIIC is negative in every window from FY2021 onward (−18.7%, −79.1%, −45.8%, −88.2%, −16.0%).

ROIC basis ROIC = NOPAT ÷ average invested capital, where NOPAT = operating income × (1 − 21%), using a constant 21% US statutory rate deliberately (Intel's effective rate ran from 20.3% to 52.8% to −119.8% to 98.3% across this window, so an effective-rate series would measure tax noise, not operations). Invested capital = total debt + total equity including NCI − cash − short-term investments − trading assets. ROIIC = (NOPAT_t − NOPAT_t−3) ÷ (invested capital_t − invested capital_t−3), rolling three-year. Cost of capital taken as roughly 9–10% (equity beta ~1.1, risk-free ~4%, equity risk premium ~5%, modest debt weight). This is a business-quality test, not a valuation of the stock.

The moat Intel actually had was never the x86 instruction set. It was process leadership — being one node ahead, so that an Intel die at the same performance was smaller and cheaper than anyone else's.▪ The FY2017 10-K said so, listing "Silicon manufacturing technologies" as a competitive strength and claiming the arrangement "reduces our costs and increases our return on capital." The FY2025 10-K makes no such claim. Owning the fabs is now defended on supply-resilience and national-security grounds. The 2017 claim was falsifiable and it was falsified.

Management claims: three "strategically important assets" — the x86 CPU franchise, advanced packaging, and the manufacturing network (CEO Lip-Bu Tan, Q1 2026 call). The 10-K's stated CCG moat is ecosystem lock-in: "Client CPUs utilizing the x86 architecture remain the foundational computing platform for the majority of PCs, enabling a heterogeneous environment from which a deep and extensive software ecosystem has developed." For DCAI it is the installed base: "The Intel Xeon installed base represents a significant portion of global server infrastructure." Note management's own verb for x86: the FY2025 10-K lists "revitalizing the x86 ecosystem" among its priorities.

External sources: the sell-side framing on file (one report, BofA, 2026-06-23) frames Intel's upside around "CY30 IDM EPS power, server CPU share, and optionality from external foundry opportunities" — so server CPU share is a pillar of the bull case. Mercury Research's data says that pillar is moving the other way: AMD went from 27.2% to 33.2% of x86 server units in four quarters and reached a record 46% of x86 server CPU revenue, while ARM took 13.2% of total server CPU shipments, roughly double a year earlier. On the client side, Intel's mobile x86 unit share went from 77.5% to 71.7% year over year and its overall x86 share from 72.9% to 67.4%, with AMD's unit shipments up nearly 17% against Intel's down more than 10% (hothardware.com, accessed 2026-07-11) [web]. The one external voice on the foundry — Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi at Intel's own 2025 customer event — said designing on Intel silicon "used to be about 2.5 to 3x more [effort]... compared to 18A, which is equivalent to the industry standard," and that customers are "desperate for optionality." Parity on design enablement and a demand for second-sourcing are table stakes.

Ground-up view: the industry structure does not permit Intel to earn excess returns from where it now stands, for four reasons that compound.

  • The ecosystem asset is non-excludable. AMD's EPYC and Ryzen are binary-compatible x86. Moving a workload from Xeon to EPYC recompiles nothing and re-qualifies no software.▪ So the ecosystem Intel funds is shared infrastructure its closest competitor consumes for free — and the speed of the two attacks measures the two switching costs exactly: AMD took 6 points of x86 server unit share in four quarters, while ARM, where migration actually costs something, took more than a decade to reach 13.2%. Against ARM, Intel has a real (shrinking) barrier. Against AMD it has none, and AMD is the one taking the share. IBM's System z is the analogue that does not hold: an installed-base moat works for IBM because the instruction set is proprietary. Intel licensed x86 to AMD, so its installed base is missing the one property — excludability — that makes an installed base a moat.
  • Minimum efficient scale is now above Intel's own volume. TSMC spread $40,900M of FY2025 capex across the whole fabless world and earned a 50.8% operating margin. Intel spread $14,646M across its own volume alone and earned roughly zero. Same capital intensity, a fifth of the volume base to amortize it over.▪ Intel's own 10-K concedes it: leading-edge nodes' "cost structure requires manufacturing volumes beyond what we expect from our own products to achieve economic efficiency."
  • Buyer power is high and vertically integrating. Dell (19%), Lenovo (12%) and HP (12%) are 43% of revenue and each ships AMD in the same SKU lineup; switching between Intel and AMD is a motherboard redesign, not an ecosystem migration. On the cloud side the buyers — Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta — are named in the same 10-K sentence as customers and as competitors building their own silicon. Intel states the outcome itself: "Our competitive position can be eroded, as it has been in the last few years."
  • The supply constraint is a share-transfer mechanism, not pricing power. When an incumbent cannot supply, the customer qualifies a second source, and qualification is the sunk, sticky part of the OEM relationship. Intel is currently paying for AMD's qualification costs by being unable to ship.

Where the evidence supports something better: in DCAI, the multi-year long-term agreements are new and real: the CFO says "most of these agreements are structured with volume and pricing, and they are usually somewhere between 3 and 5 years," and Google signed one covering Xeon and IPUs in Q1 2026. Xeon 6 was selected as the host CPU for NVIDIA's DGX Rubin NVL8. Read carefully, though, the CFO frames the LTAs as buyer supply-security ("It's good for the customer because they know where the supply is coming from"), and LTAs signed during a shortage are an artifact of the buyer's problem, not evidence of the seller's power. In Intel Foundry, advanced packaging is the one offering with customer pull, premium pricing the vendor volunteers, and a growing backlog — and it is the one place the confidentiality objection the 10-K itself names largely dissolves, because a customer can buy EMIB capacity without handing Intel its wafer IP.

Evidence tests, advantage by advantage

Claimed advantage The test Evidence Result
Scale / cost position (the IDM thesis) A unit-cost or margin gap versus peers that widens with volume Intel's gross margin 34.8% vs AMD 49.5% and TSMC 59.9%. CCG is 2.4x AMD's client revenue and earns roughly half AMD's margin per dollar fully loaded. The gap has inverted. Fails
Process / manufacturing leadership A node ahead → smaller die, lower cost, price premium Intel 7 (2017) is still about half of CCG product revenue. Core Ultra tiles are partly built by TSMC. Fails

Client unit share and mobile share both declined 5–6 points in a year. Partial — real, not Intel-specific, and eroding
Pricing power Realized price outrunning input-cost inflation Q1 2026 client ASP +16% — and CCG gross profit declined ~$94M in the same quarter. FY2025 server ASP −4% while Intel's own fabs could not meet demand. Fails — this is incomplete cost pass-through
Brand ("Intel Inside") A willingness to pay a premium for the badge Intel raised price into a 13% volume decline while AMD raised volume 25% on a +1% ASP. Fails

Intel put roughly $110bn of gross capex into the ground over FY2021–FY2025 and its operating income went from +$23,678M (FY2020) to −$2,214M (FY2025).

Segment-level conclusions

CCG earns its reported 28.9% only because it does not pay the true price of its own wafers. Fully loaded, its operating margin is roughly 8–13%, against fabless AMD's Client & Gaming segment at 19.6% — so Intel's client business is 2.4x AMD's by revenue and earns roughly half AMD's margin per dollar once the fab is charged to it.▪ In a business where scale is supposed to lower unit cost, the largest player is the least profitable.

DCAI is an eroding incumbency. It fails the share test outright (6 points of x86 server unit share lost in four quarters; ARM doubling) and the peer-returns test outright (AMD's Data Center segment earned $3,603M of FY2025 operating income against DCAI's $3,422M on $284M less revenue, and in the March-2026 quarter AMD's Data Center segment at $5,775M was larger than all of DCAI at $5,052M, on the same fiscal close date▪). The pricing-power test is more nuanced than a flat failure: FY2025's −4% server ASP came from pricing actions Intel took in H1 2025, before the supply constraint bound, and Q1 2026's +27% came after it bound. Neither is product-led pricing power, but the sequence matters and the FY2025 figure should not be presented as pricing weakness under scarcity. What survives is a default position in the enterprise socket, a migration-cost advantage against ARM but not against AMD, and a real cyclical upswing.

Intel Foundry has no advantage in the market it is trying to enter. It has never reported a positive operating income: −$7,083M (FY2023), −$13,291M (FY2024), −$10,318M (FY2025), −$2,437M (Q1 2026) — $33,129M cumulative in thirteen quarters. Its FY2025 external revenue of $307M is 0.18% of the $169.5bn foundry market, which puts it outside TrendForce's top ten, below PSMC and Nexchip. And the structure works against it: the 10-K concedes "many of the largest potential foundry customers are fabless semiconductor companies whose products compete with our own," so Intel's vertical integration is a customer-acquisition liability.▪ TSMC's founding principle was that it would never compete with its customers.

Business-model analogues

  • Boeing (commercial airplanes) — a duopoly incumbent with an enormous installed base and real customer switching costs, whose manufacturing execution broke and whose competitor took share year after year without needing a better product, only a deliverable one. The mechanism holds tightly: the moat was never the brand, it was the ability to build. Where it breaks: aircraft have a 20-year replacement cycle and a certified duopoly, so Boeing's clock is far slower than Intel's 2–3 year PC refresh.
  • Ericsson (wireless infrastructure) — an incumbent standard-holder with a large installed base that lost technology and cost leadership, retained volume share but lost pricing, and saw margins compress to single digits while management kept pointing to the installed base. This is the closest fit for DCAI. Where it breaks: Intel owns leading-edge fabs, which is an optionality Ericsson never had.
  • IBM hardware in the 1990s — a vertically integrated incumbent whose integration was the advantage until the industry disaggregated, at which point owning the factory became the liability and the profit pool moved to the specialists. This is the best analogue for Intel Foundry's drag on the product segments, and it also names the exit: IBM survived by monetizing the lock-in and shedding the fabs.
  • For Intel Foundry specifically, the closest reference class is Samsung Foundry (an IDM running a merchant foundry that competes with its own customers, structurally sub-scale, loss-making) and GlobalFoundries (the same asset base one strategic decision later: GF abandoned the leading edge in 2018 and now earns an 11.7% operating margin on $6,791M of specialty revenue). No company in the strong reference class fits.

Against the three calibration points, this is not the top tier — Intel has not held off its attackers, and AMD went from 27.2% to 33.2% of x86 server units in four quarters — and it is not quite the absence of any edge either — the x86 ecosystem and the OEM distribution are real and buy time. What separates it from an advantage that is merely eroding is that Intel's excess returns are not narrowing; they are already gone.

4. Competitive landscape & market sizing

4a. Client compute silicon

Market structure: a legally-constructed duopoly at the x86 layer inside a slightly wider oligopoly at the PC layer. The barrier that keeps ARM out does not keep AMD out.▪

Basis Intel AMD Apple Other HHI
x86 client CPU units, Q1 2026 [web, Mercury] 70.4% 29.6% — — 5,832
All PC client silicon by system units, CY2025 [estimate] ~65.8% ~22.7% 9.0% ~2.5% ~4,940

Both figures are far above the DOJ/FTC "highly concentrated" threshold of 2,500.

Market sizing, bottom-up: IDC counted 284.7M worldwide PC shipments in CY2025, +8.1% year over year. Deduct 25.6M Macs, roughly 2M Arm-Windows systems and roughly 5M Arm Chromebooks [estimate — no credible Chromebook unit disclosure was found], and x86 client systems are about 252M. At Mercury's CY2025 average shares that is roughly 187M Intel client CPUs and 65M AMD [estimate]. Management's own figure is a "client consumption TAM greater than 290 million units in 2025" — a different basis (consumption versus sell-in), about 2% above IDC's, and not worth litigating.

CY2026 is the number that matters and it is bad. Intel guides its PC unit TAM "down low double-digit percent"; IDC forecasts −11.3% for the full year with Q4 declines that "could reach 20%," driven by a DRAM/NAND shortage with no relief expected before end-2027 [web]. Intel expects to outperform that TAM: the CFO said client revenue will be "kind of flattish from Q2 onward," attributing it to "pricing a little bit, but also because of inventory replenishment at the customer level." Flat client revenue against a −11% unit TAM is an implicit forecast of roughly +11–12% client ASP for the year, and it depends on scarcity persisting.▪ It is the most falsifiable near-term claim Intel has made.

The arithmetic that defines this segment: Intel and AMD together are the x86 client CPU market, and both disclose a client revenue line, so the pool can be built from filings with no estimation:

Period Pool $M Intel client $M Intel share AMD client $M AMD share
FY2023 31,851 27,200 85.4% 4,651 14.6%

The pool grew $6,389M from FY2023 to FY2025. AMD captured $5,989M of it — 93.7%. Intel captured $400M, 6.3% of the growth in a market it entered holding 85%.▪ Intel's client revenue is flat to the dollar across the two years while the market around it compounded 9.6% a year. Mercury's independent client-revenue-share series (AMD 26.6% in Q1 2025, 31.4% in Q1 2026) corroborates the filing-derived figures to within about a point at both dates.

The counter-consensus fact in this segment: AMD now realizes a higher client CPU ASP than Intel.▪ The proof point is Q4 2025, where AMD held 36.4% of desktop CPU units and 42.6% of desktop CPU revenue [web, Mercury] — a revenue share above unit share directly implies a higher ASP. Mercury's Q1 2026 revenue-over-unit index gives AMD 31.4%/29.6% against Intel's 68.6%/70.4%, implying AMD's client ASP about 9% above Intel's, down from about 14% above a year earlier. The top-down unit build gives Intel ~$147 against AMD ~$165, the same sign. On desktops, AMD is now the premium vendor. Intel's stated strategy — the CFO on the Q4 2025 call: "within client we're focusing on the mid- and high end and not as focused on the low end" — is a strategy AMD has already executed and won.

Share counter-evidence: (1) the ASP inversion above destroys the last defensible version of the client bull case. (2) Intel is deliberately donating client units to protect DCAI, which is reversible in principle when supply recovers but means CCG is increasingly manufactured at TSMC, the same foundry AMD uses, stripping out whatever process-based cost advantage integration was supposed to confer. (3) Supply is the binding constraint and it is Intel's own fab; every unit Intel cannot ship is a socket AMD or Apple fills, and sockets are sticky for a product cycle. (4) A −11% TAM turns a share fight into a knife fight: Intel's plan is to hold revenue on price, AMD's is to take units, and both forecasts cannot be right. (5) ARM on Windows remains the threat everyone watches and AMD is the threat actually taking Intel's money — Snapdragon X was roughly 0.8% of PC shipments, and over FY2023–FY2025 Apple added about 2.6M Mac units while AMD took about $6bn of Intel's revenue pool.

Intel's share declined by two-thirds in two years without losing revenue — DCAI grew 5.9% over the same period. The market grew 3.4x around it.▪ Adding AWS's captive silicon (a run-rate above $20bn, larger than all of DCAI) pushes Intel below 6%.

Structural point: the entire x86 server CPU revenue pool runs at roughly $30.5bn annualized [estimate: Intel's disclosed $4,117M of Q1 server revenue at Mercury's 54% Intel revenue share]. NVIDIA booked $62.3bn of Data Center revenue in a single quarter. The market Intel leads is worth about one-eighth of the market it does not meaningfully serve.▪ Intel's own 10-K concedes the crowding-out: customers are "prioritizing GPU systems offered by certain of our competitors to handle compute-heavy generative AI workloads, often at the expense of CPU investment."

The Q1 2026 unit-share arithmetic, two ways: scaling Mercury's x86 shares by the non-ARM share of total shipments gives Intel 67.8% of all server CPU units in Q1 2025 and 58.0% in Q1 2026 — a 9.8-point loss in one year▪ [estimate]. Cross-check: Intel's own 10-Q discloses server volume −5% year over year while Mercury reports total server CPU shipments up more than 10%, which implies 67.8% × (0.95/1.10) = 58.6%. The two angles agree within 0.6 points, so the loss is robust, not an artifact of one dataset.

Share counter-evidence, ranked: (1) hyperscaler in-sourcing is the most structural: ARM took 13.2% of server CPU units, roughly double a year earlier; AWS says Graviton has been more than half of all new CPU capacity it has added for three consecutive years and that 98% of its top-1,000 EC2 customers use it [web]. These are Intel's largest customers building their replacements. (2) AMD holds 33.2% of x86 server units but 46% of x86 server CPU revenue, so it wins the high-core-count, high-ASP sockets; Intel's own 10-K concedes "a higher mix of lower core count products" pressured its ASPs. (3) NVIDIA is the demand sink. (4) Broadcom is entrenched in the custom-ASIC market Intel just entered. (5) Intel's own supply constraint hands away the marginal socket at the moment the installed base is being refreshed.

What is going Intel's way: Xeon 6 as the host CPU for NVIDIA's DGX Rubin NVL8; the multi-year Google LTA covering Xeon and IPUs, structured with volume and pricing; Granite Rapids traction the CFO calls "quite good"; and the custom-ASIC line, which is the fastest-growing thing Intel owns.

4c. Merchant foundry

Market structure: one of the most concentrated markets in industry, and getting more so. TrendForce puts the top-10 merchant foundry base at $169.5bn in FY2025 (+26.3%), with TSMC at roughly 70%, Samsung 7.2%, SMIC 5.32%, UMC 4.35%, GlobalFoundries 3.87%, and the rest under 3% each. HHI is 5,020 on those shares [estimate: computed from TrendForce's top-10 shares; the base excludes IDM captive output], against a DOJ "highly concentrated" threshold of 1,800. This is a monopoly with a fringe, not an oligopoly.▪ At the leading edge it is worse: TSMC's advanced technologies (≤7nm) were 77% of its 4Q25 wafer revenue (3nm 28%, 5nm 35%, 7nm 14%), implying roughly $82bn of merchant ≤7nm revenue against roughly zero for Intel [estimate]. TSMC sets price at the leading edge and there is no second source with scale.

Intel Foundry holds an estimated $92bn of net fab assets against TSMC's roughly $119bn — about 77% of TSMC's asset base — and extracts 0.19x of revenue per dollar of it against TSMC's 1.03x. TSMC gets 5.4x more revenue from each dollar of fab asset. Intel spent $89.2bn of capex across 2022–2025 and produced $1.0bn of cumulative external foundry revenue across 2023–2025: about 1.1% of the capex.▪ Meanwhile TSMC is raising 2026 capex 27–37% while Intel holds flat to down. The physical capacity gap at the leading edge is being funded to widen.

Intel Foundry's external revenue has shrunk, not inflected.▪ FY2023 $547M → FY2024 $159M → FY2025 $307M — still 44% below FY2023 three years into the foundry push. Cumulative external revenue across FY2023–FY2025 is $1,013M; TSMC books that in about three days. The apparent Q1 2026 inflection is an accounting reclassification, and the 10-Q says so: external revenue "was $174 million, up $143 million from Q1 2025, primarily due to Altera's transition to an external customer following the deconsolidation of Altera in Q3 2025." Altera was Intel's own subsidiary until 12 September 2025 and Intel still owns 49% of it. Intel did not win Altera in the market; it divested Altera and now bills it externally. The other named driver, U.S. government Secure Enclave work, is a defense-sourcing award. Backing both out, arm's-length competitive external revenue was roughly $28M a quarter in the three pre-deconsolidation quarters of 2025 [estimate: FY2025's $307M less the $222M attributed to Q4], annualizing to about 0.07% of the merchant foundry market. And the line went the wrong way sequentially: $222M in Q4 2025 to $174M in Q1 2026.

The one credible opening is advanced packaging. TSMC's CoWoS is capacity-short: 13k wafers per month at end-2023, a target of 120–140k by end-2026, with a supply-demand gap still around 20% narrowing to about 10% by end-2026 (trendforce.com, accessed 2026-07-11) [web]. When the monopolist is sold out, a second source has a reason to exist. Intel has run EMIB in high-volume manufacturing since 2017, introduced EMIB-T in 2025, and reported adding to its advanced-packaging backlog in Q1 2026. Packaging also sidesteps the confidentiality objection the 10-K itself names. The counter: no dollar figure, no named customer, and Intel already outsources some EMIB production to Amkor. Treat it as real but unsized; §20 records it as an open gap.

5. Value chain & profit pools

Intel is in the middle of a chain in which every adjacent layer earns a better return than it does.▪ Its sole-source tool supplier earns a 52.8% gross margin. The merchant foundry that is simultaneously its supplier and its principal competitor earns a 50.8% operating margin. Its memory suppliers roughly doubled their prices in a quarter. And even the PC makers — the layer usually described as commodity box-shifters — converted their PC dollar into positive operating profit in FY2025 while Intel, consolidated, ran an operating loss.

One $1,000 notebook of end-customer spend

Leading-edge wafer Intel Foundry (internal) vs TSMC (merchant) $17,826M of segment revenue, 98% intersegment Intel Foundry (58)% op margin; TSMC +50.8% [web] TSMC sets the merchant price; Intel's internal price is a transfer price

The arithmetic: per $1,000 PC, Dell's operating profit is $56. Intel CCG's segment operating profit on its ~$155 of capture is $45. Intel's consolidated operating profit on that same $155 is negative $6.50. The OEM out-earns the chip designer in absolute operating dollars per PC, and once Intel is charged for its own fabs its economic take on that PC is negative.▪

The AI-server chain is a better place to sit. In an AI rack the CPU is a small share of cost, which makes the hyperscaler price-insensitive on the host CPU. That is visible in the numbers: FY2025 server ASP was −4%, yet DCAI's operating margin went from 20% to 31% in Q1 2026 on +22% revenue. Intel is not winning the AI accelerator dollar — Gaudi was written off — but it is capturing an annuity on the host socket of racks whose economics are set by someone else's GPU. That is a better place to be than fighting NVIDIA head-on, and it is the most durable thing in the value chain right now.

The binding constraint, tested

The company map's hypothesis — Intel's own internal wafer capacity, specifically Intel 7 — is confirmed for revenue and incomplete for margin.

Confirmed: the CFO says Q1 2026 "revenue would have been meaningfully higher, but demand continues to outpace our growing supply," and put the foregone amount at a figure that "starts with a B" — at least $1bn a quarter, at least 7.4% of the quarter. Intel is increasing wafer starts on Intel 10, Intel 7, Intel 3 and 18A, which confirms Intel 7 is the binding node, not a legacy one.

Incomplete: the marginal constraint on profit has moved upstream. The CFO names memory, wafers and substrates as costs "driving higher costs that could impact demand for our product at some point in the year," and names T-glass and substrates as 2H 2026 gross-margin headwinds. The FY2025 10-K says Intel is "currently being impacted by industry supply constraints for memory chips, substrates and foundry capacity." Intel's fabs cap how many units it can sell; its suppliers cap how much it can earn on each one.▪ The Q2 gross-margin guide of 39% against Q1's 41% is that fact made numeric.

Intel un-locked itself. Capital-expenditure commitments went from $20.0bn (FY2024) to $12.8bn (FY2025), a 36% cut in the year immediately before demand outran supply. Intel cancelled or slowed Ohio, Germany, Poland, Malaysia and Israel and consolidated Costa Rica. It must now raise tool spend roughly 25% year over year in 2026 on flat total capex, against multi-quarter equipment lead times, and it is paying for the delay at $1bn-plus a quarter.

Customer-side economics

The PC OEMs are thin, falling, and the shock absorber for everyone else. Dell's Client Solutions Group earned 5.6% and HP's Personal Systems 5.3%, down from 6.2%. HP's own 10-K states it plainly: gross-margin declines reflect "increases in component and manufacturing costs... especially increasing memory and storage costs... that we are unable to pass on to our customers." This is the ceiling on Intel's new pricing power, and it is close.▪ Intel is taking pricing actions into a customer layer that earns 5–6%, is already losing margin to memory, cannot pass cost through, and is facing a unit TAM Intel itself guides down low double digits.

The hyperscalers are the opposite: price-insensitive on the CPU, and now pre-committing volume and price to secure Intel supply. That is an inversion of the last decade.

The prospective foundry customer's return does not clear — except in packaging. Intel states it has "been unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of our nodes," and the structural reason is in the same filing: most of the largest potential foundry customers compete with Intel Products. TSMC does not have that conflict. Packaging works where wafers do not, because a customer can buy EMIB capacity without handing Intel its process IP or its product roadmap.

Net effect: Intel's newly-won power over its customers is worth less than it looks, because it is passed straight through to memory makers, ASML and substrate suppliers.▪ The proof is Intel's own guidance — record demand, a supply constraint costing it $1bn-plus a quarter in revenue it would like to ship, and a gross margin guided down 200 basis points sequentially.

Circularity and financing

Intel's capital structure is now unusually entangled with its own value chain. FY2025 share count went from 4,330M to 4,994M, 15.3% dilution in one year.

Counterparty Role in the chain Instrument Size

The NVIDIA node is the strangest object in the chain: simultaneously the competitor whose accelerators displaced Intel's data-center franchise, a roughly 4% shareholder, a customer (Xeon 6 is the host CPU for DGX Rubin NVL8), and a co-development partner. Intel's recovery in DCAI is now partly financed by the company that caused its collapse.

The cash round-trip: Intel raised $7.0bn of strategic equity and took $5.7bn of accelerated CHIPS money — then spent $14.2bn buying Apollo out of Fab 34. The strategic capital raised was more than consumed by unwinding a prior financing partner. Net of all of it, Intel diluted holders 15.3% and Q1 2026 adjusted free cash flow was still −$2.0bn.

And the 14A trigger ties the whole chain together. If Intel cannot land a significant external 14A customer it says it "may pause or discontinue" leading-edge development — an action it describes as potentially "effectively irreversible" — which would simultaneously impair a substantial majority of $100bn-plus of net PP&E, forfeit government incentives and possibly require repayment, trigger penalty payments to Apollo and Brookfield under the SCIP agreements, and make Intel Products permanently dependent on TSMC, with which it has no long-term contract. Every financing counterparty and every supplier is on the same trigger.

6. Secular & industry trends

Intel's end-markets all grew and Intel's revenue did not.

2015 2025 Change
Global semiconductor market $335,200M ~$772,000M +130% (8.7% CAGR)
Intel net revenue $55,355M $52,853M (4.5)%
Intel's share of the industry 16.5% 6.8% (9.7) pts

(Industry size from SIA/WSTS [web]; Intel revenue from the FY2016 and FY2025 10-Ks.) Held at its 2015 share, Intel would have reported roughly $127bn of revenue in 2025 [estimate: 16.5% × $772bn]. It reported $52.9bn. That $74bn gap is the secular story in one number, and it is not cyclical: Intel's revenue peaked in FY2021 and has declined 33.1% since, through a period in which the industry grew every year.▪

A note on the TAM figure management quotes. On the Q1 2026 call the CEO said the industry TAM is "approaching $1 trillion." WSTS's Spring 2026 forecast is $1.51tn for 2026 [web], but almost the whole upward revision is memory price inflation. Intel exited NAND and never sold DRAM. The TAM management cites is inflated by the one part of the industry Intel is not in.

Decomposing the $26.2bn decline from the FY2021 peak: roughly $4.3bn is the NAND divestiture and roughly $1.9bn is Altera, leaving about $19.9bn — 76% — of organic decline, split almost evenly between CCG (about $10.8bn) and DCAI (about $9.9bn). This is not a portfolio-pruning story with a healthy core underneath. Both cores shrank by about the same amount.▪

PC: a replacement market on a plateau, into which Intel is losing share. PC unit shipments went 348.8M (2021), 292.3M (2022), 252.0M (2023), 262.7M (2024), 284.7M (2025), and IDC forecasts 252.5M in 2026 (−11.3%) [web]. The 2025 growth was Windows-10 end-of-support and COVID-fleet aging — Intel's own 10-K says so — and that driver is now spent. Intel's revenue capture per PC shipped went $107.5 (2023) → $109.2 (2024) → $97.0 (2025), an 11.3% decline in one year. With client ASPs flat by Intel's own disclosure, that gap is units.

The AI PC is a mix lever, not a volume lever.▪ AI PCs are more than 60% of Intel's client CPU mix and AI PC revenue grew 8% sequentially in Q1 2026. Over the same period Intel's client revenue declined from $28,700M to $27,600M and its revenue capture per industry PC declined 11.3%. Nothing in the external unit data supports an AI-PC supercycle: IDC's 2026 forecast is −11.3% units and Intel's own TAM guide is down low double digits.

Data center: the market grew roughly 14x and Intel's revenue in it did not grow at all. Intel's data-center revenue went from $15,981M (DCG, 2015) to $16,919M (DCAI, 2025) — a 0.6% CAGR over ten years, on a broader definition than the old DCG series. Over the same window NVIDIA's Data Center revenue compounded from $339M to $193,700M. Intel's share of the merchant data-center compute pool went from roughly 98% to 7.4% [estimate: DCAI ÷ (DCAI + NVDA DC + AMD DC); the true figure is lower still because it excludes Broadcom's AI ASICs and all captive hyperscaler silicon]. This is the central secular fact about Intel and it cannot be undone by a good server year.▪

The CPU:GPU attach argument, tested: management's core forward case is that AI inference and agentic workloads move the CPU:GPU ratio from 1:8 toward parity. The trend is real and independently observed — Mercury attributes part of AMD's record revenue share to this shift. But the attach ratio governs Intel's unit count, not its share of the dollars. Even at a 1:1 attach, an AI rack pairs a server CPU costing a few thousand dollars against an accelerator costing tens of thousands. NVIDIA's data-center revenue is $193,700M; Intel's entire DCAI is $16,919M with $3,422M of operating income. Doubling the attach ratio roughly doubles Intel's AI-attached host-CPU units and still leaves Intel with a single-digit share of the AI compute dollar. The trend is favourable and the conclusion drawn from it does not follow.

How much of DCAI's +22% is cycle and how much is trend: industry x86 server units grew more than 10% year over year; Intel's server unit share declined about 6 points to AMD and further to ARM; pricing actions and rising core count were positive; the custom-ASIC line contributed; and networking was folded into DCAI by the Q1 2025 recast. The market finally grew faster than Intel's share loss. That is worth a lot in the near term and says nothing about 2030.

Intel Foundry is levered to the strongest secular trend in semis and has captured about 0.17% of it. The 10-K's own framing is the strongest secular claim in the document — "demand for leading-edge foundry capacity has increased significantly to support the demand for compute, particularly from AI workloads" — plus the shift from monolithic chips to chiplets integrated through advanced packaging, plus supply-chain regionalization. Every part of that is true. External foundry revenue is $307M against a top-10 foundry market running near $185bn annualized. Being levered to a trend you cannot sell into is a cost, not an asset, until a named 14A customer appears.▪

Policy: the CHIPS Act became an equity stake, and China is in structural decline. The Department of Commerce took 275M shares, a warrant for 241M at $20.00, and 159M escrowed shares; Intel received $5.7bn of accelerated disbursements and its milestone conditions were removed. Separately, China revenue went from $15,532M (FY2024) to $12,694M (FY2025), −18.3%, and from 29.2% to 24.0% of revenue, while U.S. revenue rose 21.3% to $15,757M. That re-basing is policy, not demand, and it is structural.

The input-cost shock is new since the FY2025 10-K and it changes the 2026 slope in both segments. IDC models PC ASPs +18.3% and units −11.3% in 2026, with no meaningful relief from the memory shortage before end-2027 [web]. Memory is a large share of a PC's bill of materials, so a large memory price increase raises system prices, destroys unit demand, shrinks Intel's unit TAM, and raises Intel's own input costs. It hits the top line and the gross margin at the same time. It is a cyclical shock, but its magnitude is enough to dominate 2026, and it arrives as the Windows-10 refresh rolls over.
