7. Critical points

1. The consolidated operating loss is the only real margin number, and the segment table does not contain it. Intel Foundry's revenue is 98.3% intersegment, booked at prices "intended to approximate market pricing." CCG's 28.9% and DCAI's 20.2% FY2025 operating margins are therefore struck after paying an internal price to a manufacturing arm that lost $10,318M charging it. Intel Products "earned" $12,739M of operating income; consolidated Intel posted a $2,214M operating loss. If the transfer price does equal market, Intel's cost of manufacture is roughly 58% above market and CCG's margin exists only because another segment absorbs the gap.▪ Intel discloses no segment assets and states it is "impracticable to determine" segment depreciation, so nobody outside the company can test the split. Move the transfer price by 6% of Intel Foundry's revenue and more than $1.0bn moves between the two.

2. Intel's price/volume relationship inverted between FY2025 and Q1 2026, and a model anchored on FY2025 is modelling the opposite business. For the whole of FY2025 Intel sold more server units at lower prices (+9% volume, −4% ASP) — the behaviour of a share-defending price-taker. In Q1 2026 it sold fewer units at much higher prices (−5% volume, +27% ASP), and the same inversion happened in client (−13% volume, +16% ASP). The rate limiter on Intel's revenue is now its own fab output. But price taken under scarcity is not the same asset as price won on product: in CCG the 16% ASP increase produced negative incremental gross profit, and the 10-Q attributes the pricing to offsetting "higher input costs."

3. Intel Foundry has produced no operating leverage in two years. Excluding impairments, the quarterly operating loss has sat in a $2,320M–$2,509M band for five consecutive quarters while quarterly revenue grew 16% year over year; across nine quarters revenue grew 23% and the loss is unchanged. Q1 2026 is the cleanest data point and the most damaging: revenue grew 16.2% year over year and the operating loss widened, from $2,320M to $2,437M.▪ The 10-Q's explanation is that the growth itself is loss-making at the margin — "$489 million of unfavorable impacts related to lower product profit in Q1 2026 due to an increased mix of higher cost wafers manufactured on our Intel 18A process node." And $34,543M of construction in progress is not yet depreciating, which adds roughly $4.3bn a year of depreciation as it enters service.

4. The 14A gate resolves in the second half of 2026, and it is the only truly binary thing in the file.▪ The FY2025 10-K states Intel has "been unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of our nodes" and that absent a significant 14A customer it "may pause or discontinue" leading-edge development — an action it calls potentially "effectively irreversible," triggering impairments against $100bn-plus of net PP&E, loss and repayment of government incentives, and penalty payments under the SCIP agreements. The CFO said on the Q4 2025 call that customers' window to secure 14A capacity "will be in the back half of this year." The disclosure has since softened: the Q1 2026 10-Q rewrote the test from an external-customer test to a "sufficient committed demand... through product design wins with potential significant external customers and our Intel products roadmap" test, and Intel has moved more of its own tiles onto 14A.

5. The consensus operating-income line requires Intel Foundry to swing $10–12bn, and no published estimate says so. Bloomberg publishes no segment consensus for Intel. But running CY2029 consensus operating income of $21,955M through Intel's own segment structure — giving the street its own bullish assumptions of a 30% Intel Products margin and improved corporate unallocated — leaves Intel Foundry at roughly breakeven [estimate: §14]. Even at a 36% Products margin, a level Products has never printed, Intel Foundry must still cut its loss by two-thirds. There is no path to the consensus number in which Intel Foundry keeps losing anything like what it loses now.

6. Depreciation is the most under-modelled line in the company. FY2025 depreciation was $10,757M, up 37.1% in two years while Intel Foundry's revenue declined 3.7%. The $34,543M of construction in progress adds roughly $4.3bn a year at full run-rate on an 8-year machinery life. Consensus takes gross margin from 34.8% to 53.0% by CY2030 — an 1,820 basis point climb — straight through the period this depreciation arrives. The sharper test is cash gross margin: consensus implies roughly 73%, at or above Intel's all-time best, with double the depreciation burden and no process leadership. In FY2016–18 Intel printed a 71–72% cash gross margin with process leadership, a fully-depreciated fab base, and no TSMC line in its own bill of materials. Today it buys compute and GPU tiles from TSMC.

7. Minority partners have a growing, permanent claim on Intel's earnings that no consensus line captures. Non-controlling interest equity went from $0 in FY2021 to $12,079M at FY2025 and $13,595M at Q1 2026. Management guides NCI income to roughly $250M per quarter for Q2–Q4 2026 and ~$1.1bn in each of 2027 and 2028 — 13.2% of consensus CY2027 net income. In a low-profitability scenario the minority partners take more than the entire earnings of the company. And the SCIP structures are equity-labelled but debt-shaped: Apollo put $11,000M into Ireland SCIP in Q2 2024 and Intel bought it back for $14,200M in April 2026, a roughly 15–17% annualized cost against Intel's own 4.20% bond coupon, with the $3,565M cash difference charged to equity and appearing in no income statement.

8. Intel is the only company in its own compensation peer group that lost money, and the annual bonus paid about 120% of target. The committee replaced the group operating-income metric with an operating-expense metric for FY2025, set the revenue target below the prior year's actual, set a PSU revenue-growth target of negative 2%, and made operating expense the only metric capable of paying 200% — which it did. R&D declined $2,772M (16.8%) and MG&A $883M (16.0%) in the year. There is no ROIC, ROIIC, free-cash-flow or operating-income metric anywhere in the annual bonus or the long-term plan, at a company holding $100bn-plus of net PP&E whose entire investment question is whether that capital earns a return. The long-term equity, by contrast, has bitten hard: 2022 PSUs paid 0%, Gelsinger's realized pay was about 20% of his headline pay, and Tan's new-hire PSUs require the stock to triple to reach target.

9. The stock's move is mostly multiple, and the sell-side has not raised its estimates to match. From the FY2024 year-end, Intel's 5.48x price move factors into 1.48x of forward earnings and 3.71x of multiple — roughly three-quarters is re-rating. From the January-2020 peak the stock is +72% while 12-month-forward consensus EPS is −73%. Consensus CY2028 adjusted EPS is lower today ($2.454) than it was fifteen months ago ($2.665) while the stock is 5.5x higher. Forty-nine analysts model FY2027 and the high estimate is 6.6x the low. The mean published price target of $103.26 is below the $109.84 price and the modal rating is Hold. (See §15.)

10. Advanced packaging is the one credible external-revenue path in the company, and it is entirely unsized. Management moved its own demand estimate up an order of magnitude in eighteen months, from "hundreds of millions of dollars" to "billions of dollars per year," says pricing is "very attractive relative to some of the other areas of the foundry business," and expects revenue from 2027 — while declining to give a number when asked directly. No backlog figure, no capacity number, no named customer, and Intel has already begun outsourcing some EMIB production to Amkor. This is the most important undisclosed number at Intel (§20).

8. Variant perceptions

Each point below disagrees with how management, the sell-side, or the segment table frames the issue.

V1 — "The products business earns 26% margins; it's the foundry that's broken." Consensus framing: CCG's 28.9% and DCAI's 20.2% prove a healthy fabless-equivalent business trapped inside a bad fab. Evidence against: those margins are struck after paying Intel Foundry an internal transfer price on 98.3% of its revenue, and Intel itself says the segments "are meant to reflect separate fabless semiconductor and foundry companies." Fully loaded, CCG earns roughly 7.9%–12.9% against fabless AMD's 19.6%, and DCAI earns roughly −0.8% to 6.8% on FY2025 [estimate: allocating the $10,318M Foundry loss on revenue, cost and silicon-area weightings]. The direction of any bias in the transfer price is not determinable from disclosure — Intel provides no segment assets and no segment depreciation — so the segment margins cannot be independently tested,, not being demonstrably overstated. Quantification: the reported-to-fully-loaded bridge for CCG is $9,317M → $2,551M–$4,158M, a $5.2–6.8bn overstatement of the client business's economic profit.

V2 — "Intel has regained pricing power: client ASP +16%, server ASP +27%." Evidence against: both are scarcity rents produced by Intel's own wafer shortage, and one is provably uneconomic. In CCG the 16% ASP increase delivered negative incremental gross profit — the change in cost of sales was +$192M against a change in revenue of +$98M, so gross profit declined about $94M. All of CCG's operating-income improvement came from headcount cuts. The 10-Q says the pricing was taken "in part to offset higher input costs." Price that does not expand gross profit is not pricing power. Quantification: if the FY2026 ASP gains reverse to flat by FY2028, not compounding, FY2030 operating income declines roughly $3.6bn on the server leg alone.

V3 — "Intel Foundry's external business is inflecting." Consensus framing: $174M in Q1 2026 was 57% of the entire FY2025 external figure in one quarter. Evidence against: the 10-Q attributes it "primarily due to Altera's transition to an external customer following the deconsolidation of Altera in Q3 2025" — a 49%-owned related party buying under a wafer supply agreement. The same wafers, to the same buyer, relabelled because Intel sold 51% of the customer. And the line declined sequentially, from $222M in Q4 2025. FY2023 external revenue was $547M, 78% higher than FY2025's $307M. Quantification: backing out Altera and U.S. government work, arm's-length competitive external revenue was roughly $28M a quarter in the three pre-deconsolidation quarters of 2025 [estimate] — about 0.07% of the merchant foundry market. The statistic is arithmetically true and economically empty.

V4 — "The Foundry turnaround is working; the loss narrowed 22% in 2025." Evidence against: $2,350M of the $2,973M improvement — 79% — is a smaller impairment and accelerated-depreciation charge ($3,300M in FY2024 to $950M in FY2025), a non-cash accounting item. Real cost cuts of $1,200M were two-thirds offset by $849M of new 18A ramp inventory reserves. Net operational improvement: roughly $350M on a $10.3bn loss. Quantification: excluding impairments the quarterly loss has been −$2,320M, −$2,368M, −$2,321M, −$2,509M, −$2,437M across the last five quarters, flat within a ±4% band, while quarterly revenue grew 16% year over year.

V5 — "DCAI's margin recovery is operating leverage returning." Evidence against: incremental margins of 253% (FY24→FY25) and 104% (Q1'25→Q1'26) are only possible when costs decline in absolute terms. In Q1 2026 DCAI's cost of sales plus opex declined 1.2% ($3,551M → $3,510M) on 22.4% revenue growth. Intel's own MD&A attributes FY2025's gain to "$1.5 billion of favorable impacts related to lower operating expenses, primarily driven by lower payroll-related expenditures as a result of headcount reductions," plus lower Gaudi charges, and states the revenue benefit "was substantially offset by higher server unit costs." Restructurings do not repeat, and management already guides 2026 opex above its own ~$16bn target. Quantification: of DCAI's $2,477M two-year operating-income improvement, roughly $1,500M is disclosed opex reduction and a further roughly $547M is the swing in Gaudi inventory charges ($922M → $375M) — together more than the total increase. Revenue growth contributed approximately zero.

V6 — "The CPU is back, and Intel is the beneficiary." Evidence against: the CPU market is back; Intel's position in it is still eroding, and eroding faster in value than in units. In the very quarter DCAI grew 22%, AMD's server CPU revenue share reached a record 46%, and AMD's Data Center segment ($5,775M) overtook all of Intel DCAI ($5,052M) on the same fiscal close date, growing 57% against Intel's 22%. Intel's share of all server CPU units declined from roughly 67.8% to 58.0% in one year, confirmed two independent ways within 0.6 points. Quantification: had Intel held unit share, Q1 2026 server volume would have been roughly +10%, not −5%; at the disclosed ASP that is about $600M of forgone quarterly server revenue, or $2.4bn annualized.

V7 — "Adjusted free cash flow of −$1.6bn shows the cash burn is nearly over." Evidence against: Intel's "adjusted free cash flow" nets government incentives and SCIP partner contributions out of capex. On the unadjusted GAAP definition (operating cash flow less gross capex), FY2025 free cash flow was −$4,949M, three times worse. Over FY2022–FY2025 GAAP free cash flow was −$44,295M against Intel's adjusted −$19,768M. The $24,527M gap is $4,524M of government incentives plus $19,333M of SCIP partner contributions — and the SCIP money is a financing inflow that creates a permanent NCI claim on the fabs' future output, not cash Intel generated. Quantification: NCI equity went from $0 to $12,079M in four years, and NCI already took $293M of FY2025 income.

V8 — "Smart Capital worked: Intel got the government, Apollo, Brookfield, SoftBank and NVIDIA to fund the fabs." Evidence against: the offsets did land — $24,471M on $93,594M of FY2022–FY2025 gross capex, 26.1%, squarely inside management's stated 20–30% target. But the price of the money was never marked. Apollo's $11,000M cost $14,200M to redeem 22 months later, roughly 15%/yr against about 5% on Intel's own notes, plus a $755M derivative charge. The equity was sold at $20.00–$23.28, the cheapest prices in a decade. Quantification: roughly $3,200M of realized excess cost on Apollo alone; the 580M shares issued in 2025 for $12,706M are worth about $63.7bn at $109.84. So the offsets worked and the strategy still failed. Offsets reduce the capital at risk; they cannot make a fab economic if the wafers do not sell.

V9 — "Intel keeps missing." Evidence against: it has not, for three years. Revenue beat consensus in 11 of the last 12 quarters (mean +3.7%), adjusted EPS in 9 of 12, and management has beaten its own guide six quarters running by a widening margin (+3.6%, +4.1%, +9.3%, +4.6%, +3.0%, +11.5%). The market has not paid for it: the median next-session reaction to those twelve prints was −1.3%, and 7 of 12 were negative. Quantification: every large negative reaction (Q4 2023, Q1 2024, Q2 2024, Q1 2025, Q2 2025, Q4 2025) followed a guide below the street, and five of those six came with a revenue beat. The stock trades on the guide and the structural question, not the print.

V10 — "The bull case is the good outcome for shareholders." Evidence against: only partly. The bull case is the one that triggers the U.S. government's 241M-share warrant at a $20.00 strike, because the warrant becomes exercisable precisely when Intel drops below 51% ownership of Intel Foundry — which is what a separation, a spin, or an anchor customer taking equity in Foundry would do. The event that validates the bull case is the event that dilutes the holders who bet on it. Separately, the escrowed government shares are a share-settled derivative marked through "interest and other, net," so a rising Intel share price mechanically produces P&L losses: $1,796M in FY2025 and a further $1.1bn in Q1 2026 alone. Quantification: the warrant alone is roughly +4.4% of shares. Every GAAP EPS line in any model is overstated in the scenarios where the stock appreciates.

Five key inflections:

  • The process failure surfaces, and the financials lag it by three years (2018–2020). Intel's revenue and free cash flow were at all-time highs in the very year the moat broke: FY2020 produced $21,605M of free cash flow, the largest in company history, and Bob Swan called it "the best year in our company's history, our fifth record year in a row" on the same call that disclosed the 7nm defect. Only gross margin showed the deterioration. It had already declined 5.7 points from FY2018 and would decline for four more years. Any account that dates Intel's decline to the FY2022 revenue collapse is three to four years late.

  • IDM 2.0: the chosen bet (February–March 2021). Gelsinger reversed the fabless off-ramp Swan had been signalling and committed to building a merchant foundry. Average operating margin went from 31.3% across FY2018–FY2020 to 1.6% across FY2021–FY2024. Cumulative capex FY2021–FY2025 was $107,917M against cumulative operating income of $7,991M — capex was 13.5x the operating income it was spent alongside. Cumulative free cash flow went from +$73,843M (FY2017–FY2021) to −$44,295M (FY2022–FY2025). Intel committed to a ten-year, $100bn-plus capital cycle on a merchant-foundry thesis it had not tested with a single significant customer, and five years on the 10-K states it still has none.

  • Capitulation: the dividend and the workforce (2024-08-01). Intel suspended a dividend it had paid every year since 1992, cut more than 15% of the workforce, and announced a $10bn-plus cost programme. It was forced and it was late: free cash flow had already been negative for three consecutive years (−$9,411M, −$14,279M, −$15,656M) while Intel paid out $5,997M, $3,088M and $1,599M of dividends funded by debt and asset sales.

  • Leadership change and the reversal of the capex thesis (December 2024 – March 2025). Tan cut FY2025 capex 38.8% ($23,944M → $14,646M) and R&D 16.8% ($16,546M → $13,774M), and the 10-K confirms Intel "delayed or cancelled manufacturing facility construction or expansion projects in Ohio, Germany, Poland, Malaysia and Israel." FY2025 was the first year since FY2017 in which gross margin increased. This is the third strategic direction in seven years — Swan's pragmatic outsourcing, Gelsinger's IDM 2.0 double-down, Tan's conditional retrenchment. Intel's capital cycle is ten years long; its strategy cycle is three.

  • State recapitalization and the demand/supply inversion (August 2025 – Q1 2026). Intel sold roughly 10% of itself to the U.S. government and took strategic money from a named competitor. Simultaneously the operating constraint inverted: for the first time in a decade Intel's revenue is limited by its own fab output, not by customer preference. Tan on the Q1 2026 call: "A year ago, the conversation about Intel was about whether we could survive. Today, it's about how quickly we can add manufacturing capacity." That is a change in kind, not degree. The foundry thesis that justified the $107,917M of capex remains unproven by Intel's own admission.

How Intel behaves, from the record:

  • Bad news is disclosed incrementally and in the mildest available framing. The 7nm defect was disclosed as a six-month product slip while the underlying process was twelve months behind. The dividend was halved twice before being suspended. The Gaudi target was reaffirmed in Q1 2024 and abandoned in Q3 2024.
  • The dividend and the strategy story are defended past the point the cash flow supports them. Intel paid $5,997M of dividends in FY2022 on −$9,411M of free cash flow.
  • Crown jewels are monetized under duress, and each sale is filed under strategy. McAfee, NAND, the Mobileye IPO, IMS minority stakes, 49% of two fabs, 51% of Altera, and ultimately about 10% of the company to the U.S. government — all filed in the FY2023 10-K under "Optimize our Portfolio and Unlock Value."
  • Metrics that flatter appear, and disappear when they stop. "Lifetime deal value" was introduced on the Q4 2023 call as "probably the best metric that we can give you," with a promise of "periodic updates." It appears in exactly four transcripts and in zero of the six calls since Q4 2024. It was never reconciled and never withdrawn. External foundry revenue declined 71% in the year management said the pipeline doubled from $4bn to $10bn-plus.
  • "Five nodes in four years" and "process leadership" appear 54 times across 14 calls through Q3 2024, and zero times since. The phrase disappeared the quarter Gelsinger left. The "60% gross margin / 40% operating margin" long-term model has not been repeated since Q2 2024.

10. Management, incentives & capital allocation

10a. Leadership

Four CEOs in eight years: Krzanich (2013–2018, resigned), Swan (2018–2021), Gelsinger (2021–2024, resigned under board pressure), Tan (since 2025-03-18). David Zinsner, CFO since January 2022, is now the longest-tenured member of senior management at a little over four years. That is the tenure floor of the whole team.

Justin Hotard, hired from HPE in February 2024 to run DCAI — the segment now inflecting — departed after about thirteen months to become CEO of Nokia; the DCAI leadership seat has turned over roughly four times since 2020. Christoph Schell resigned effective 30 June 2025 with no severance and no bonus. Michelle Johnston Holthaus, the passed-over internal candidate for CEO, was granted a letter agreement on 28 February 2025 — days before Tan's appointment took effect — entitling her to severance "in the event she resigned for good reason... within two years following our appointment of a new CEO." She exercised it seven months later. Separately, Intel's company-wide undesired turnover was 7.9% in 2025 against 5.9% in 2024 (10-K, Human Capital); note this is a voluntary-departure rate for all regular employees, not an executive metric.

The price of getting manufacturing talent in is the mirror image. Naga Chandrasekaran's July 2024 offer letter provides, on top of the Executive Severance Plan, two payments declining from $7,000,000 and $6,000,000 — up to about $13M of severance protection for a non-CEO hire, to bring a Micron executive in to run Intel Foundry.

10b. The FY2025 incentive plan

Metric Weight (Tan) Threshold (0%) Target (100%) Max (200%) Achievement (adjusted) Score
Revenue 25% $48.0bn $52.0bn $58.0bn $53.36bn 113.6%
Gross margin % 25% 34% 37% 40% 36.96% 99.6%
Operating expense 25% $19.5bn $18.5bn $17.5bn $16.48bn 200%
Intel Top Jobs 25% — — — Products 88.5 / Foundry 72.5 72.5–88.5%

Final payouts: Tan 118.7% ($2,374,000); Zinsner 120.7%; Chandrasekaran 119.1%; Johnston Holthaus 120.3%. In a year with a $2,214M GAAP operating loss, a $(0.06) diluted EPS and $(1,612)M of adjusted free cash flow, executives took home roughly 119–121% of target cash bonus.

Three design features produced that outcome. First, the profit metric was removed: the committee "replaced the group operating income performance metric with a new company operating expense metric," so the annual plan contained no profit measure other than gross-margin percentage. Second, targets were set below the prior year's actual — the proxy says the expectation of a revenue decline "factored significantly into the committee's decision to set a 2025 target goal for revenue lower than... the actual result for revenue in 2024" — and the PSU revenue-growth target was set at −2.0%. Third, the single metric that maxed out was operating expense (scored on an adjusted basis), and the spending reduction that accompanied it came predominantly from research: R&D declined $2,772M, or 16.8%, and MG&A $883M, 16.0%. Intel 14A, the node the 10-K says Intel may have to abandon, is an R&D programme.

The long-term plan's cash metric scores on cash flow from operations, which is struck before capital spending: it paid its maximum in a year adjusted free cash flow was −$1,612M — the outcome the CEO himself called "completely unacceptable" on the Q2 2025 call. There is no ROIC, ROIIC, free-cash-flow or operating-income metric anywhere in the annual bonus or the long-term plan.

The plan's adjustments also credited executives with revenue Intel no longer owned: achievement was adjusted "to reflect what would have been achieved had Altera continued to be fully owned by Intel through the end of fiscal 2025 and achieved the results forecasted for the remainder of 2025," which flips reported revenue growth from −0.5% to +0.5%. And the disclosed payout cannot be reproduced from the disclosed inputs: linear interpolation from the adjusted $53.36bn achievement gives 122.7%, while the proxy discloses 113.6% (which implies the reported revenue figure). The difference favours shareholders, so it is not evidence of inflation, but the disclosed inputs do not reproduce the disclosed payout.

Tan's own package is the strongest part of the system. His new-hire PSUs pay 0% if the stock does not rise, and target (100%) requires a 200% increase in the stock price; maximum requires 300%. He was required to purchase $25M of stock with his own money on 21 March 2025 and must hold it through every vesting date. He has no cash severance. His ownership guideline is 10x salary against 5x for every other named executive.

And the long-term equity has bitten. The 2022 PSUs paid 0% of target. The 2023 PSUs paid 76%. No named executive exercised an option or had a PSU vest in FY2025. Gelsinger's compensation actually paid was −$78.5M in 2022 and −$82.2M in 2024; across 2021–2024 his cumulative realized pay was about $46.0M against about $234.5M of Summary-Compensation-Table totals, roughly 20%, and he forfeited all unvested equity including his new-hire awards on departure.

Pay versus performance, and the peer group: $100 invested in Intel at end-FY2020 was worth $85.08 at end-FY2025; the same $100 in Intel's compensation peer group became $264.83 — about 180 points of underperformance in five years, over which revenue declined 29% and net income went from +$19.9bn to −$0.3bn, while average non-PEO named-executive pay rose 22%. The peer group is seventeen technology companies including Amazon, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft, NVIDIA and Meta, and Intel's own proxy discloses its standing inside it: 36th percentile on revenue, 0th percentile on net income. Intel is the only loss-maker in its own comparator set. Say-on-pay support ran below 50% for three consecutive years (2020: 41%, 2021: 38%, 2022: 34%), recovered above 88% in 2023–24, and declined to 72% in 2025.

Ownership: all fifteen current directors and executive officers together own 2,749,994 shares — about 0.05% of Intel. The U.S. government holds 433,323,000 shares (8.4%), roughly 158x more than every insider combined. Tan is the exception, and it is contractual: 1,226,377 shares, almost all of it the $25M he was required to buy and is required to keep. The Board also amended the stock-ownership guidelines effective 1 January 2026 in ways that each lower the bar: unvested RSUs now count toward the requirement (they previously did not), measurement moved from at least quarterly to every two years, and the measurement price moved from a 30-day to a 12-month average.

Candor is sharply improved from a low base. Tan's Q2 2025 prepared remarks repudiate his predecessor's core strategy in plain words: "the capacity investment we made over the last several years were well ahead of demand and were unwise and excessive"; "Our last full fiscal year of positive adjusted free cash flow was 2021. This is completely unacceptable"; "I do not subscribe to the belief that if you build it, they will come." He matched words to actions — Germany and Poland cancelled, Costa Rica consolidated, Ohio slowed. This is the most candid Intel commentary in the ten-year transcript record, and it is a sitting CEO grading his predecessor's capital allocation in public.

10c. The ten-year capital-allocation record

Intel committed 141% of its ten-year operating cash flow to three programmes at once — a fab build-out, two mega-acquisitions, and a full shareholder-return programme — and funded the gap by selling assets, selling stakes in its own factories, and finally selling equity in itself at the cheapest prices in a decade.

Intel's capex sits across three cash-flow lines — an investing line, a second "additions to property, plant and equipment" line inside financing for capex on extended payment terms ($3,026M in FY2025), and held-for-sale NAND PP&E. Gross capex FY2025 = $14,646M + $3,026M = $17,672M, exactly the figure the CFO gave on the Q4 2025 call. Any capex series taken from the XBRL investing line alone understates FY2024 and FY2025.

Total uses of $305,274M against $216,704M of internal cash is an $88,570M shortfall, closed with $85,365M of external funding. What that bought: revenue down 11.0%, operating income from +$13,133M to −$2,214M, EPS from $2.12 to −$0.06, and shares outstanding up 5.6% (4,730M → 4,994M) despite $47,152M of buybacks. Every per-share line went backwards.

Diluted per share 2016 2020 2025

Operating income / share $2.69 $5.59 $(0.49)
FCF / share $2.50 $5.06 $(1.76)

Returns on the capex programme: cumulative gross capex FY2016–FY2025 of $181,173M against a −$15,347M change in operating income, i.e. −8.5%. Even on the FY2016 → FY2021 window, before the collapse and after $87,579M of capex, the change in operating income was +$6,323M — +7.2% on the capex, below any plausible cost of capital in the good years. Write-offs against the deployed capital: $3,300M of manufacturing-asset impairments and accelerated depreciation in FY2024 (a substantial majority on Intel 7), $950M in FY2025, $3,100M of goodwill and intangible impairments in FY2024, $3,900M more on Mobileye in Q1 2026, and a $9,900M deferred-tax valuation allowance in FY2024 — an accounting acknowledgment that Intel did not expect to earn enough U.S. taxable income to use its deferred tax assets.

The buyback record is the inverse of the discipline management claimed.

FY Spent $M Avg price paid INTC avg price that year INTC low that year
2016 2,587 ~$30 $33.33 $28.22
2018 10,730 $49.96 $49.05 $42.42
2019 13,576 $49.93 $51.38 $43.46
2020 14,229 $51.82 $54.89 $44.11
2021 2,415 $61.12 $55.85 $47.89
2022–2025 0 — $18.13 (2025 low)

Pace rose monotonically with the price. The final purchase — 39.5M shares at $61.12 in Q1 2021 — was the highest price Intel ever paid and the last repurchase it ever made. It then bought nothing while the stock traded down to $18.13, and in 2025 issued 580M shares at $20.00–$23.28 to raise $12,706M. Intel retired about 990M shares at roughly $47.62 and re-issued more than half of them at roughly $21.91.

Two years before it needed every dollar of that capital for the fab programme, Intel committed in writing to fund a $20bn buyback partly by selling assets. CEO Bob Swan, Q3 2019 call: "We'll fund the buyback from proceeds we generate from partnerships and/or noncore asset dispositions and by returning approximately 100% of 2020 free cash flow to investors," having just said Intel "returned 100% free cash flow to shareholders over the last 10 years." Intel executed $16,644M of the pledge (FY2020 $14,229M at $51.82; Q1 2021 $2,415M at $61.12) and then stopped permanently.

The "Smart Capital" offsets landed and the strategy still failed. At the February 2022 Investor Day the CFO said offsets would be "about 10%" of gross capital investments but "in reality, we are chasing 20 to 30." Actual: 26.1% of FY2022–FY2025 gross capex. The plan's revenue leg missed by a mile — a targeted 10–12% revenue CAGR against an actual FY2022→FY2025 CAGR of −5.7%.

And the offsets are now being unwound at a cost. Apollo put $11,000M into Ireland SCIP in Q2 2024; Intel bought the 49% back on 8 April 2026 for ~$14,200M cash (funded with $7,700M of cash and a $6,500M 364-day term loan at 4.79%), having already taken a $755M charge in Q4 2024 on the liquidated-damages derivative for construction delays it chose to make. Intel paid $3,200M more than it received, 22 months later — roughly 15%/yr on $11,000M of financing, against senior notes that cost about 5%. §12 tests the CFO's "highly accretive" framing.

Under Tan, one inflection and one reversal: capex declined from $25,122M (FY2024) to $17,672M (FY2025), adjusted free cash flow turned positive in H2 2025 (+$3,100M), and management guides positive adjusted free cash flow for FY2026 — but only "excluding the buyout of the Fab 34 joint investment," a ~$14,200M outflow. And capex guidance has moved "down" → "flat to down" → "flat" in three quarters, with equipment spend guided up ~25% year over year. The discipline is being tested in its first up-cycle and is already bending. Still no buybacks and no dividend in the fifth year, with $7.2bn of authorization unused since Q1 2021.

11. M&A, divestitures & deal track record

Intel is a value-destroyer in M&A, and the record is unusually clean-cut because the money is concentrated in two deals. Of roughly $34bn of acquisition cash deployed from FY2015 through FY2025, about $30bn — 88% — went into Altera and Mobileye. Both were bought at multiples several times Intel's own: Altera at about 8.6x trailing sales, Mobileye at about 41x. Both were sold or written down. Neither produced the integrated product that justified the price. Roughly $9bn was destroyed on Altera and $8bn on Mobileye, before counting the decade of R&D Intel funded inside each. (Cross-reference §10 for the aggregate uses of cash; this section owns the deal detail.)

Roughly $9bn destroyed over ten years

The synergy track record: both mega-deals stated large, dated, checkable synergy targets and both stopped reporting against them. Altera's product synergies were 60% of the stated deal value — an integrated Xeon+FPGA in up to a third of cloud nodes by 2020, opening an $11bn incremental market. Neither the product nor the attach rate ever appeared, and Intel simply stopped mentioning the targets. Mobileye's case was a ">$70bn TAM by 2030" plus about $175M of cost synergies; the TAM has not been referenced in current filings and the cost-synergy tracking stopped. The one target Intel did explicitly withdraw was Gaudi's $500M, on the Q3 2024 call — which is the acknowledgment the others never got.

The goodwill and impairment record: Mobileye's $10,278M of recorded goodwill has been impaired by roughly $6,500M, most recently $3,900M in Q1 2026, driven by "the sustained decline in Mobileye's market capitalization" and booked to corporate unallocated, not to a segment. Goodwill remaining across the company is $23,912M.

The Altera headline valuation does not reconcile to Intel's own mark. Every press account says the Silver Lake transaction "values Altera at $8.75 billion." But Intel fair-valued its retained 49% at $3,246M by reference to "Altera's equity value per the terms of the transaction agreement," which implies roughly $6.6bn for 100%. The likely reconciliation is enterprise value versus equity value — Silver Lake levered Altera at close — but Intel never reconciles the two, and any comparison of the $8.75bn headline to the $16.7bn paid understates the destruction.

The counter-evidence, and its limits: the NAND exit to SK hynix was well-timed and cleanly executed. IMS Nanofabrication is the one acquisition in the ledger that visibly compounded — bought inside about $913M of 2015 acquisitions, then marked at roughly $4.3bn when Intel sold a 32% minority stake for $1.4bn in 2023 to Bain Capital and TSMC. But its purchase price was never separately disclosed, so the return cannot actually be computed, and it is by far the smallest deal in the ledger.

Since 2021 Intel has been a net seller, monetizing roughly $24bn of assets while acquisition spend collapsed to $13M (FY2023), $82M (FY2024) and nil (FY2025). That is prudent given the record, but it means the portfolio is being liquidated to fund the fabs, not optimized. The open question the ledger raises: given the pattern of selling down Mobileye into weakness and the 14A capital requirement, is Mobileye the next asset sold to fund the fabs?

12. Capitalization & balance sheet

Intel's reported balance sheet looks conservative and its economic balance sheet does not. The funded debt stack is well-built — long-dated, cheap, no financial maintenance covenants, a modest near-term ladder. Intel will not be forced into a refinancing by its bonds. The balance-sheet risk is in three places invisible in "total debt": the SCIP structures, the capex programme against negative free cash flow, and equity dilution as the funding mechanism of last resort.

The debt stack

Every instrument is a fixed-rate senior unsecured note or a municipal-style industrial-development bond. There are no convertibles, no secured debt, and zero commercial paper outstanding against a $10.0bn authorized programme. Summarized by maturity bucket (the full 42-instrument schedule is in the FY2025 10-K, Note 13):

Weighted-average cost of debt (computed) Principal-weighted coupon: 4.20% — the cash-pay basis, implying $1,982M of annual cash interest on the FY2025 stack. Weighted-average effective rate: 4.59% — the P&L basis, including premium/discount and issuance-cost amortization. The 39 basis-point gap is real: the 3.73% Dec-2047 note has a 6.17% effective rate, and the 4.90% Jul-2045 note a 6.52% rate. Weighted-average maturity: 16.1 years, on a final-maturity basis. Fixed at the instrument level: 100%. Effective floating exposure after swaps: ~$9.7bn (~21%) [estimate: inverted from the 10-K's own disclosure that +1% on rates costs +$97M of annual interest].

$1,437M of the stack is remarketable or puttable — the Oregon and Arizona industrial-development bonds have mandatory tender dates in 2027–2029, so they behave as short paper even though they are documented out to 2049–2052. A failed remarketing is a funding event.

The April 2026 re-levering — a subsequent event in no reported balance sheet

On 8 April 2026 Intel reacquired Apollo's 49% of Ireland SCIP for ~$14.2bn cash, funded with about $7.7bn of existing cash and a $6.5bn 364-day senior unsecured term loan at 4.79%, which Intel "intend[s] to refinance, subject to market conditions."

FY2024 FY2025 Q1 2026 reported PF Apr-2026
Total debt $M 50,011 46,585 45,031 51,531
Cash + short-term investments $M 22,062 37,416 32,789 25,089
Net debt $M 27,949 9,169 12,242 26,442
Non-controlling interests $M 5,762 12,079 13,595 13,453
Net debt + NCI $M 33,711 21,248 25,837 39,895

Against an FY2025 EBITDA proxy of $8,543M (operating loss of $2,214M plus $10,757M of D&A): reported net debt/EBITDA of 1.07x becomes 3.10x pro forma, and net debt plus NCI over EBITDA is 4.67x. One caveat: FY2025 EBITDA is depressed and inflecting up, and if EBITDA recovers toward $15bn these ratios roughly halve. The point is not that Intel is over-levered today. It is that the reported 1.07x was never the real number: reported net debt declined from $27.9bn to $9.2bn in FY2025 because $17.8bn of equity-classified cash came in from Apollo, Brookfield, the U.S. government, SoftBank and NVIDIA, not from cash generation. The agency that downgraded Intel from BBB+ to BBB in August 2025, citing "execution risks tied to our technology roadmap and foundry strategy, delayed deleveraging and weaker than expected demand," was right in direction: eight months later net debt is back to roughly $26.4bn pro forma.

The 2027 wall is bigger than management's stated commitment. The CFO said on the Q1 2026 call: "We remain committed to retiring all $2.5 billion of maturities as they come due this year and all $3.8 billion in 2027." That commitment covers the bonds only. The $6.5bn term loan matures around April 2027 and is not in the $3.8bn. The actual 2027 cash requirement if the term loan is not refinanced is $3,826M + $6,500M = $10,326M. Intel says it intends to refinance, and at the current BBB curve that is likely achievable — but it is a real call on the market inside twelve months and Intel's first refinancing need in a decade.

The SCIPs: equity-labelled, debt-shaped

Both SCIPs are consolidated variable-interest entities. Partner cash comes in as non-controlling interest and capital in excess of par value, so it increases equity and reduces reported net debt, while the partner's economic claim behaves like senior, expensive capital against a specific fab.▪

Ireland (Apollo) — a completed round trip, so it can be priced. Apollo put in $11,000M (Q2 2024) and took out $14,200M (April 2026) plus $365M of interim distributions: a 1.32x money multiple over about 1.85 years, an implied 15%–17% annualized return [estimate: the exact Q2 2024 close date is not disclosed; a 1.8–2.0 year holding period is used], against Intel's own 4.20% coupon and the 4.79% term loan raised to fund the buyback. The $3,565M net cash cost of the round trip is charged to capital in excess of par value and appears in no income statement, in no EPS figure, and in no "total debt" line.

Testing the "highly accretive" framing: annual cost of funding the $14.2bn: $311M on the term loan at 4.79%, plus roughly $308M of forgone yield on the $7.7bn of cash redeployed [estimate: ~4.0%, the 10-K's SOFR-tracking investment yield] = $619M. Annual benefit: Ireland SCIP NCI income no longer shared — $268M on FY2025 actuals, or $540M at the Q1 2026 annualized run-rate. Break-even requires Ireland SCIP NCI income above about $619M a year. At the Q1 2026 run-rate the deal yields 3.8% on the $14.2bn purchase price against the 4.79% cost of the debt funding it: roughly break-even in year one, and accretive only on a forecast of rising Fab 34 earnings. The disclosed numbers support something narrower than "highly accretive": unwinding the structure now is defensible because the financing was expensive and the fab is ramping. The expensive decision was entering the structure in 2024, and that cost is locked in.

Arizona (Brookfield) — the same structure, larger, and still open. The NCI balance went $874M (Dec 2022) → $2,359M → $3,888M → $9,106M (Dec 2025) → $11,353M (Mar 2026), with contributions accelerating: $5.1bn in FY2025 and another $2.1bn in Q1 2026 alone. The production contract commenced in Q1 2026, so Intel is now "required to both operate Arizona SCIP at minimum production levels and limit excess inventory held on site or we will be subject to certain volume-related damages" — a take-or-pay obligation on Intel's own fab output, converting a demand shortfall into a cash penalty. $18.8bn of Intel's PP&E ($5.8bn of construction in progress plus $13.0bn in service) is on the balance sheet but is "not available to us as [it] can be used only to settle obligations of the VIE." Management guides NCI income to roughly $1.1bn in each of 2027 and 2028 — almost all Brookfield now — a permanent, growing leak of consolidated earnings away from Intel shareholders. If Intel unwinds Brookfield on the Ireland precedent the cash call is roughly $14.5bn [estimate: 1.29x contributed capital; the Ireland price was negotiated, not formulaic, so this is an order of magnitude only]. Nothing obliges Intel to do it, and Intel has now demonstrated that it will. The filings disclose no put, no call and no formula, which makes this the largest unquantified balance-sheet exposure at the company (§20).

One reason the NCI line cannot be used as the measure of the partners' claim: Ireland SCIP's NCI book value was $142M against an exit price of $14,200M, a 100x gap, because consolidation accounting eliminates substantially all of the VIE's assets and liabilities. Any leverage or book-value analysis that uses the NCI line as the partners' economic claim is wrong by two orders of magnitude.

From 2015 to 2020 Intel retired 14.0% of its shares on $47.7bn of repurchases. From 2020 to Q1 2026 the count rose 23.7% on zero repurchases. FY2025 alone added 664M shares — the largest single-year dilution in Intel's history — across the U.S. Department of Commerce (275M), SoftBank (87M at $23.00), NVIDIA (215M at $23.28) and employee plans.

Contingent dilution not yet in the count: roughly 150M escrowed shares (released at a $20.00 basis as Secure Enclave disbursements are received; if the eligibility period ends with shares unreleased, half go to the Department of Commerce for free and half are cancelled, so a floor of about 75M more shares is issued regardless of performance), plus the 241M-share warrant at a $20.00 strike, exercisable only if Intel ceases to own at least 51% of Intel Foundry. Fully-diluted ceiling: 5,414M shares, +33% versus the 2020 trough of 4,062M. The warrant is a structural block on the most-discussed strategic option: every foundry-separation thesis runs into a right for the U.S. government to buy 241M shares at $20.00, which at $109.84 is roughly $21.6bn of latent value transfer at the moment the strategy is deemed to have worked.

The escrowed-shares derivative has negative convexity. It is share-settled and marked to market through interest and other, net: fair value went from $2.7bn (Dec 2025) to $3.6bn (Mar 2026), producing $1,796M of losses in FY2025 and a further $1.1bn in Q1 2026 alone. A rising Intel share price mechanically produces P&L losses. The accounting was restated after an SEC staff consultation concluded in Q4 2025, so any figure on this topic taken from the Q3 2025 10-Q is stale.

Liquidity, leases, pension, interest

Cash and short-term investments were $32,789M at Q1 2026, or roughly $25.1bn pro forma for the Apollo payment. Committed facilities have shrunk $5.0bn (33%) since FY2024: the 364-day revolver went $8.0bn → $5.0bn → replaced by a three-year $3.0bn facility, alongside an untouched $7.0bn five-year revolver. A full-text search of the FY2025 10-K returns no financial maintenance covenants on the notes or the revolvers — a material strength, because Intel posted a $19.2bn net loss in FY2024 without tripping anything. New in Q1 2026: $1.7bn of contractually enforceable customer deposits, i.e. customers pre-paying to reserve capacity.

Leases and pension are immaterial and should not consume model time: total present value of lease payments $473M; pension projected benefit obligation $2,657M against $2,198M of plan assets, a $459M net unfunded position. Intel owns its fabs outright.

Interest expense is a mechanical headwind hiding inside capitalized interest. Reported FY2025 interest expense was $1,091M — but Intel capitalized $1.2bn of interest into fab construction ($1.5bn in each of FY2024 and FY2023). Gross interest incurred was $2,291M, which reconciles to the computed 4.59% effective rate on an average debt balance of $48–50bn. This reverses. As construction in progress is placed in service and capex moderates, the capitalizable base shrinks and reported interest expense rises toward the gross figure — before adding $311M for the new term loan. Pro-forma gross interest is roughly $2.6bn a year, more than double the $1,091M FY2025 reported line. Note also that FY2025's positive $3,257M of "interest and other, net" is an artifact of the $5,553M Altera divestiture gain; strip it and the line is a $2,296M loss.

Structural balance-sheet risks

  1. The Brookfield/Arizona SCIP obligation — $11.4bn of NCI and rising, take-or-pay volume commitments now live, $18.8bn of PP&E ring-fenced. A roughly $14.5bn cash call to unwind on the Ireland precedent, plus about $1.1bn a year of earnings leakage. Leading indicator: Arizona partner contributions in the quarterly NCI note.
  2. Capex against negative free cash flow. 2026 capex guided flat to 2025; Q1 2026 gross capex was $5.0bn against $1.1bn of operating cash flow. Management guides positive adjusted free cash flow for FY2026 excluding the $14.2bn Fab 34 buyout — which means, including it, 2026 free cash flow is deeply negative.
  3. The $6.5bn 364-day term loan, maturing around April 2027 and not covered by the CFO's stated commitment. Total 2027 need is $10.3bn if not refinanced.
  4. Equity dilution as the funding mechanism of last resort. Up 23.7% since 2020, with about 391M more contingent shares not in the count.
  5. The Intel 14A "pause or discontinue" clause, which fires through the SCIPs. A 14A failure means Intel slows construction, which breaches SCIP construction and volume commitments, which triggers penalty payments (Intel has already paid this once, $755M to Apollo in Q4 2024), which lands alongside impairment against $104.5bn of net PP&E and a further downgrade. Every link in that chain is disclosed in the FY2025 10-K, and the structure is pro-cyclical by design: the things that go wrong together are wired together.
  6. Structural subordination. The senior notes "will effectively rank junior to all liabilities of our subsidiaries," and the subsidiary count is rising (Mobileye ~80%, IMS 68%, Arizona SCIP 51%).

Ten-year shape in one line: revenue peaked at $79,024M in FY2021 and is down 33% to $52,853M. Gross margin declined 26.2 points from 61.0% to 34.8% and declined in every one of the seven years from FY2018 to FY2024, with no year of respite — while revenue kept rising for three of those years.▪ Gross margin was the leading indicator; revenue was the lagging one. Operating margin went from 22.1% to −4.2%; ROIC from 18.3% to −1.3%. Invested capital grew 82% ($74,394M → $135,529M) while NOPAT went from $10,375M to −$1,749M. The dividend, paid continuously since 1992, was cut in FY2023, cut again in FY2024, and paid at zero in FY2025. Buybacks stopped after FY2021.

What the KPIs show: two regimes. From FY2016 to FY2021 Intel held price and lost or held units — monopoly-rent behaviour, punctuated by the FY2020 COVID notebook spike. From FY2022 the collapse: notebook volume down 36% and server volume down 16% in FY2022 alone, server volume down a further 37% in FY2023. FY2024–FY2025 shows Intel oscillating — cutting server price to buy volume in FY2025 (+9% units, −4% price), then reversing in Q1 2026 (−5% units, +27% price) once its own fabs became the constraint. A model anchored on FY2025's volume-led, price-cutting mix would be modelling the opposite of the business Intel has today.

Segment gross margin and the notebook/desktop split are both discontinued, and are shown here through their last disclosure. Segment gross margin was disclosed through the FY2024 10-K (CCG 52%, DCAI 47%) and is no longer derivable after the Q2 2025 change in what the CODM reviews. The notebook/desktop revenue split was disclosed through FY2024 ($19.1bn / $9.7bn) and is now a single "client revenue" line.

One new metric arrived in Q1 2026 and should be treated with care: management stated that "our collective AI-driven businesses now represent 60% of revenue and grew 40% year-over-year." It is management-defined, appears for the first time in Q1 2026, is reconciled to no reportable segment, and cannot be reproduced from the segment table (CCG +1% y/y, DCAI +22%, Intel Foundry +16% — no combination grows 40%). Treat it as narrative, not data.

14. Expectations: internal vs. external vs. base rates

Management has stopped giving full-year guidance and has beaten its 90-day guide six quarters running, while the street's five-year path requires Intel Foundry to swing $10–12bn to roughly breakeven — an outcome no published estimate states and no company in the reference class has produced.

14a. The internal record: a 90-day word and a three-year word

Intel's quarterly guidance is conservative and reliable; its multi-year guidance has been worth nothing. The same team beats its 90-day guide 73–77% of the time and has missed every multi-year target it has ever set.▪

Metric vs guide midpoint Pairs (Q4 2020 – Q1 2026) Beat Miss Mean deviation

Non-GAAP gross margin 20 13 (65%) 7 −0.3 pts (+1.6 pts excluding two quarters where impairments were booked into COGS after the guide was issued)

And the beat margin is widening, not converging: +2.3% mean across Q4 2020–Q4 2024, then +6.0% across the last six quarters (all positive), and +11.5% in Q1 2026 — $0.9bn above the top of the guided range. Tan stated the philosophy in Q&A: "as usually my style is under promise, over delivering." The other available explanation is that supply, not demand, sets the number and Intel keeps under-forecasting its own fab output. Both are in the primary record; either way, the guide is a floor, not a central estimate.

The base rate of Intel hitting its own multi-year model is 0 for 11 lines.▪ It was never formally retired; it was simply never mentioned again, and Intel has not held an investor day since. One qualifier: the current management team has not published a multi-year model and has not been given the chance to miss one.

Targets that have been abandoned or gone quiet: full-year guidance itself (discontinued from January 2023, still not resumed 14 quarters later); the dividend; "#2 foundry by 2030"; the Gaudi $500M target; "five nodes in four years" (three of five delivered, 20A cancelled); and "lifetime deal value." Intel Foundry breakeven "exiting 2027" is the only hard multi-year financial target left, and it has not appeared in earnings-call prepared remarks since January 2025 — only in conference Q&A, offered by the IR head. The hedge added in November 2025 makes it unfalsifiable: the CFO now says a stronger external win "could count against us on the profitability side... which would push the profitability out a bit."

14b. What the outside view says

Screening BBG panels: semiconductor cyclicals whose revenue declined 20%-plus from their peak regained it within five years 54% of the time with a median forward five-year revenue CAGR of +10.2%. Fallen large-cap incumbents that lost a core franchise regained it 4% of the time, with a median CAGR of +0.5%. Which class is Intel in? The panel answers it: from FY2021 to FY2025 the 20 USD-reporting semis in the panel grew revenue +80% (+20% excluding NVIDIA) while Intel's declined 33%. Intel's share of the panel's revenue went from 34.6% (2015) to 9.7% (2025). Its decline happened through an industry boom. It is share loss, not the cycle, and the fallen-incumbent class is the governing one.

Two named structural precedents that a cross-sectional screen cannot show. First: no company that lost leading-edge logic process leadership has ever regained it. IBM paid GlobalFoundries $1.5bn to take its chip unit; AMD spun out its fabs and went fabless (and recovered by doing the opposite of Intel's strategy); GlobalFoundries halted all 7nm development in 2018; UMC stopped below 14nm; Texas Instruments retreated to analog on trailing nodes and now earns a 34.1% operating margin. Zero of six regained leadership; the survivors survived by retreating to a defensible node or market. Second: no IDM has ever built a leading-edge merchant foundry of scale.▪ Intel Custom Foundry, launched in 2013, was shut in 2018 — this is Intel's second attempt. Samsung has been trying for twenty years and holds 7.2% share. The only leading-edge merchant foundry in history is TSMC, which was a pure-play from its first day and never had product customers to compete with.

Where the bull case earns credit: Intel did execute the process roadmap this time. Intel 18A entered high-volume manufacturing in late 2025 with gate-all-around and backside power, and shipped backside power in volume ahead of TSMC. Intel's own history of missing node targets has improved materially, and that is the fact most in tension with everything above. What has not changed is the commercial consequence: no significant external foundry customer, and a $10,318M segment operating loss.

And the reference class is biased in consensus's favour. A Bloomberg ticker panel contains only companies that still exist. Freescale, Xilinx, Altera, IDT, Cypress, Toshiba memory, Elpida and Qimonda are absent because they were acquired or failed. Every recovery base rate quoted above is therefore biased upward; the true rates are worse.

14c. The invested-capital arithmetic nobody does

Even if the whole consensus path lands — record revenue, the best margins since 2019 — the return on the capital base is ordinary:

Invested capital $M NOPAT at 15% tax $M Implied ROIC
FY2025A 159,071 (1,882) ~0%
FY2026E ~162,759 7,548 4.6%
FY2027E ~168,227 10,792 6.4%
FY2028E ~174,080 15,774 9.1%
FY2029E ~180,189 21,631 12.0%

[estimate: invested capital rolled forward at consensus capex less D&A of $12.5–14.0bn; 15% tax rate; no buybacks and no further impairments. Note this uses the wider invested-capital definition (debt + equity − cash only), which runs about $23bn above the definition used in §3; on the tighter definition the ROIC levels are correspondingly higher, but the conclusion does not change.]

TSMC earned 26.8% in FY2025 and has not been below 17.8% in a decade. The reference class recovers ROIC to a median 12.7% at t+5. So the consensus ROIC outcome is exactly the median of the base rate, while the margin and growth inputs it takes to get there are at the maximum. The inconsistency has one cause: the capital base is so large that even an unprecedented P&L recovery only produces an ordinary return.

"Perfect-foresight" forward P/E is the fiscal-year-end price divided by the next year's actual GAAP EPS; it uses hindsight and is labelled as such. "n/m" where the EPS denominator is at or below zero; the price level is still shown.

For six years (FY2016–FY2021) Intel was priced as a stable, cash-generative incumbent: a 9.5x–23x trailing GAAP multiple, a 10x–14x forward multiple, 5.6x–8.4x EV/EBITDA and 2.2x–3.3x book. The ten-year median next-twelve-month forward P/E is 13.1x. That regime ended in FY2022. At the FY2024 year-end Intel was at 0.89x book and had traded as low as 0.70x book (2024-09-06). It is now at 4.95x book and 105.8x next-twelve-month earnings.

15b. What the market learned, and when

A price move factors exactly into a change in forward earnings and a change in the multiple paid for them (endpoints internally consistent, next-twelve-month basis):

Window Price NTM consensus EPS NTM forward P/E Share of the log move from the multiple
Jan-2020 peak → now $63.92 → $109.84 (+72%) $5.01 → $1.34 (−73%) 12.8x → 81.7x (+541%) the multiple did all of it, and more
FY2024-end → now $20.05 → $109.84 (+448%) $0.91 → $1.34 (+48%) 22.0x → 81.7x (+271%) 77%
Apr-2025 trough → now $20.09 → $109.84 (+447%) $0.50 → $1.34 (+171%) 40.4x → 81.7x (+102%) 41%
FY2025-end → now (2026 YTD) $36.90 → $109.84 (+198%) $0.63 → $1.34 (+112%) 58.2x → 81.7x (+40%) 31%

From the FY2024 year-end, the 5.48x price move factors into 1.48x of forward earnings and 3.71x of multiple. Measured only from the April-2025 trough, or only across 2026, estimate revision does more of the work, because the near-term earnings base was depressed and has since recovered. Both statements are true, and any claim that "the numbers are following the stock" has to say which window it means. The top row is the one bulls and bears will argue over: from the January-2020 peak the stock is +72% while forward earnings are −73%.

Corroborating from a different direction: consensus CY2028 adjusted EPS is lower today ($2.454) than it was fifteen months ago ($2.665, at 2025-04-30), while the stock is 5.5x higher. Near-term estimates have recovered off a depressed base; the market's estimate of Intel's long-run earnings power has not gone up at all.

What the market actually reacted to, for every move beyond ±5%

Quarter Reaction What the market reacted to
Q2 2023 +6.6% Intel returned to profit after two loss-making quarters; adjusted EPS $0.13 against a consensus loss of $0.04. The Q3 guide was accepted
Q3 2023 +9.3% Beat and raised: the Q4 guide midpoint of $15.1bn at ~46% gross margin was above the street
Q4 2023 (11.9)% Beat, then guided down. The Q1 2024 guide of $12.7bn and ~44% gross margin came in well below the street. The print was ignored; the guide was the news
Q1 2024 (9.2)% An in-line print with a Q2 guide of $13.0bn and ~43.5% gross margin, below expectations again
Q2 2024 (26.1)% The capitulation quarter, and the only revenue miss in the twelve. Dividend suspended; ~15,000 roles cut; a Q3 guide at ~38% gross margin with negative EPS
Q3 2024 +7.8% A big miss with a positive reaction: adjusted EPS −$0.46 against −$0.03, GAAP EPS −$3.88. The stock rose because revenue beat 2.0% and the Q4 guide of $13.8bn / ~39.5% gross margin was above consensus. The market treated the charges as backward-looking and the guide as a floor
Q1 2025 (6.7)% Beat the print, but Tan's first call paired it with an unusually wide Q2 range and an $11.8bn midpoint below the street
Q2 2025 (8.5)% Revenue beat 8.2% but adjusted EPS missed on impairments, and the Q3 guide came with a ~36% gross margin. The margin, not the revenue, was the problem
Q4 2025 (17.0)% The clearest beat-and-lower of the twelve. Q4 beat revenue, gross margin (140bp above guide) and EPS. The reaction came entirely from the Q1 2026 guide: a $12.2bn midpoint against a $12,523M consensus, gross margin guided down to ~34.5%, breakeven EPS against a $0.06 consensus, and a capex walk-back ("previously, we said CapEx would be down, but are now planning for a range of flat to down slightly"). The stock had already risen 11.7% the session before, so the two-day move was −7.2%, not −17.0%
Q1 2026 +23.6% Beat on every line and guided far above. Revenue beat the guide midpoint by 11.3%; non-GAAP gross margin of 41.0% was 650bp above guide; adjusted EPS $0.29 against a breakeven guide. DCAI +22% y/y. The framing that moved it: "demand continues to outpace our growing supply." The GAAP line was a −$0.73 loss and the market disregarded it entirely

The pattern across all ten: the print has almost never been the news. Every large negative reaction followed a guide below the street on revenue, gross margin or both — and five of those six came with a revenue beat. Every large positive reaction followed a guide at or above the street, including Q3 2024, where the print itself was a large miss.

Forty-nine analysts model FY2027 and the highest estimate is 6.6x the lowest. On the FY2027 numbers alone the implied multiple ranges from 37x to 244x. There is no consensus on Intel's earnings power — there is an average of sharply disagreeing views. And the years that matter most are the least covered: 54 analysts model CY2026, six model CY2029 and five model CY2030, yet the stock is 45x CY2028 and 24x CY2030. Those five are self-selected: the CY2030 revenue low ($86,849M) sits above the CY2029 mean ($82,485M).

The street's own view, reported as theirs and not adopted: mean price target $103.26, i.e. 6.0% below the 2026-07-10 close; consensus rating 3.55 on Bloomberg's 1–5 scale, modal rating Hold; 18 Buy / 35 Hold / 2 Sell across 55 analysts; target high $200, low $45 (a 4.4x spread). Short interest is 127.8M shares (2.5% of shares outstanding) at 1.0 days to cover, so this is not a squeeze. Named recent moves: BofA raised its objective to $160 (Buy) on 2026-06-23; HSBC to $200 (Buy) [web]; Cantor Fitzgerald to $150 but held at Neutral [web]. Four target aggregators disagree with each other — Bloomberg $103.26, MarketBeat $97.88, StockAnalysis $93.12, ChartMill $85.09 — and every one of them is below the market price, with Hold as the modal rating.

Intel's +198% year-to-date and +361% one-year price performance are among the strongest in the universe but not the strongest: Micron is +243% year-to-date and +695% over one year, UMC is +210% year-to-date, and Samsung is +370% over one year. And Intel's 101x FY2026E adjusted P/E and 32x FY2026E EV/EBITDA are the highest of any profitable semiconductor name in the table other than Arm, a pure-IP licensor with a structurally different model. No inference is drawn from either; the table is context.

A currency note that would otherwise silently corrupt the table: Bloomberg's market-cap field is in the trading currency and in units, while enterprise value, net debt and EBITDA are in the reporting currency and in millions. EV/EBITDA and net-debt/EBITDA are therefore computed in the reporting currency (self-consistent) and only the displayed enterprise value is converted to dollars; EPS is pulled with the fundamental currency overridden to the trading currency so that P/E is currency-consistent.

17. Forward model summary

*This is an operating model only — revenue through free cash flow. No valuation, no multiples applied, no price target. Year 0 is FY2025A, tied line for line to the financial history in §13. *

17a. The three scenarios

FY2030E Revenue 5-yr CAGR Gross margin Operating income Op margin GAAP EPS FCF (OCF − gross capex)
Bear $50,745M (0.8)%/yr 39.0% $1,791M 3.5% $(0.28) $(1,092)M
Base $74,345M +7.1%/yr 45.0% $12,055M 16.2% $1.49 $10,934M
Bull $104,278M +14.6%/yr 51.0% $30,982M 29.7% $4.20 $27,566M
Consensus (BBG) $95,468M +12.6%/yr 53.0% $28,460M 29.8% $4.18 GAAP / $4.62 adj $16,515M (EBITDA − capex)

Consensus is not the base case; consensus is the bull case.▪ On revenue it is between base and bull; on operating margin and EPS it is on the bull.

17b. The driver tree

Revenue is built bottom-up as units times ASP by segment, never as a top-down CAGR.

  • CCG = client CPU units × client ASP + other CCG, where units = PC unit TAM × Intel's share of PC CPU units
  • DCAI = server CPU units × server ASP + other DCAI (networking, IPU, custom ASIC), where units = x86 server unit market × Intel's x86 server share
  • Intel Foundry enters consolidated revenue only as its external line — the $17,519M of intersegment revenue eliminates on consolidation. Consolidated cost is therefore modelled from its real drivers (unit cost, depreciation, input costs), not from transfer prices, and the segment operating margins are a reconciliation, not an input. CCG's reported 29% and DCAI's 20% are not used as model drivers anywhere.
  • All Other = Mobileye + IMS (Altera deconsolidated 2025-09-12)

The estimated FY2025 unit base: Intel discloses no absolute unit count in any period, so the entire units × ASP decomposition comes from a triangulated base: roughly 185M client CPUs at ~$149 and roughly 13.9M server CPUs at ~$1,012 [estimate; §1]. The ASP changes are disclosed and anchored; the levels are estimates with ±5% bounds that widen forward. Every unit-level projection in this model is medium confidence at best.

17c. The implied-share check, which constrains every scenario

A units × ASP model will happily produce a market share above 100% if you let it. Every scenario was run back through the market data.

Intel share of PC CPU units FY2025A FY2028E FY2030E
Bear 65.0% 57.5% 53.0%
Base 65.0% 61.5% 59.2%
Bull 65.0% 62.6% 60.3%
Intel share of x86 server CPU units FY2025A FY2028E FY2030E
Bear 71.2% 60.7% 55.3%
Base 71.2% 63.0% 60.4%
Bull 71.2% 68.6% 65.6%

All three scenarios have Intel losing share for seven straight years.▪ They differ only in the pace: the bear extrapolates the observed rate, the base roughly halves it, the bull assumes it slows sharply but does not stop. There is no scenario in which Intel takes share back, because nothing in the evidence supports one.

The model's output depends on two assumptions the evidence does not support.

Intel Foundry external revenue is not bounded on the downside. From $307M in FY2025, the bear's $2,400M implies a 7.8x increase (+51%/yr for five years) and the base's $7,600M implies 24.8x (+90%/yr). Against that: the FY2025 10-K states Intel has been "unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of our nodes"; the series is going the wrong way (Q1 2026's $174M was down from $222M in Q4 2025) and is attributed primarily to Altera, a 49%-owned related party; and the base rate for the IDM-to-leading-edge-merchant-foundry transition is 0 for 5-plus. A scale check on the base's own stated mechanism (advanced packaging only): $7,600M of external packaging revenue in FY2030 would exceed Amkor's entire FY2025 revenue of $6,708M — the world's second-largest OSAT — built from roughly zero in five years, on an unquantified CFO estimate. The evidence supports a bear of $300–800M, a base of $2,000–3,000M and a bull of $8,000–10,000M. This is the model's second-largest sensitivity ($7,300M of FY2030 operating income between bear and bull), so truncating the downside at $2,400M hands the bear roughly $950M of FY2030 operating income it has not earned.

Depreciation is scaled to the revenue scenario, and scaled backwards. Cumulative FY2026–30 gross capex is $96,500M in the bear against $96,000M in the base — the bear spends more and books less depreciation in every year. Both scenarios inherit the same $34,543M of construction in progress and the same 8-year machinery life. Depreciation follows the gross asset base, not revenue. Two consequences: the bear receives roughly $1,300M a year of operating income it did not earn (73% of its entire FY2030 operating income of $1,791M), and its $14,600M is below the arithmetic floor the model's own logic computes ($10,757M in FY2025 plus ~$4,300M a year from the CIP wave = $15,057M) before a single dollar of the $96.5bn of capex the bear itself spends. The base level of $15,900M is defensible; the scenario structure is not. Evidence supports $15.5–17.5bn in FY2030 in every scenario, spread by the timing of construction-in-progress entering service and by capex, not by revenue.

Correcting both takes the bear's FY2030 operating income from +$1,791M to roughly −$0.5bn: the bear, corrected, never reaches operating profitability.

Among the assumptions flagged weak, four matter most. Server ASP +29% in FY2026 would be, by a factor of 2.6, the largest server ASP increase Intel has ever disclosed (the decade maximum is +11%, in FY2024), and the CFO explicitly downplayed the lever: "ASPs... it's not the biggest driver, obviously, of our revenue outlook. We think the unit volume is going to be the biggest driver." The model does the opposite. Client ASP +11.5% in FY2026 is arguably too low, not too high: Q1 2026 printed +16% on a partial quarter of pricing actions and the CFO said Q2 gets "a full quarter." The steady-state ASP assumptions bank the entire FY2026 scarcity rent permanently and compound on top, taking client ASP to $185 by FY2032 (+24% versus FY2025) while the same model has Intel shedding six points of unit share to a competitor that discounts. And FY2030 gross margin of 45% implies a cash gross margin of 66.4%, which requires Intel to recover 78% of the cash gross margin it has lost since FY2020 while, in the same model, losing share in both segments and continuing to buy tiles from TSMC.

17e. Where the base case departs from consensus

Three lines account for the whole $16.4bn gap between the base FY2030 operating income ($12,055M) and consensus ($28,460M).

Gross margin: consensus takes gross margin to 53.0% by CY2030. In 30 years of the semiconductor panel, P(gross margin ≥ 50% at t+5 after a collapse) = 0 out of 28. But the sharper test is cash gross margin:

Gross margin Depreciation / revenue Implied cash gross margin
FY2018A 61.7% 10.6% 72.3%
FY2020A (last good year) 56.0% 13.5% 69.5%
FY2025A 34.8% 20.4% 55.2%
Base, FY2030E 45.0% 21.4% 66.4%
Consensus, CY2030E 53.0% ~20% [est] ~73.0%

Consensus asks Intel to run a cash gross margin at or above its all-time best, with double the depreciation burden and no process leadership.▪

Depreciation: in the base, depreciation stays at 20–22% of revenue through FY2032, against 10–11% in FY2016–18. One caution in the other direction: Intel has already pulled this lever once — effective January 2023 it extended the useful life of certain production machinery from five to eight years, cutting FY2023 depreciation by an estimated $4.2bn. A further extension is available and would flatter the P&L without changing a dollar of cash.

Intel Foundry: the base takes Intel Foundry from −$10,318M to roughly −$1.6bn by FY2030 — an $8.7bn improvement, most of the way — and still lands 58% below consensus operating income. Put Intel Foundry at exactly breakeven and the base operating income becomes about $13.7bn, still less than half of consensus's $28,460M. The consensus gap is not a foundry gap. It is a revenue-and-product-margin gap that a foundry turnaround alone cannot close.▪

17f. Free cash flow — the line that decides everything

$M FY2026E FY2027E FY2028E FY2029E FY2030E
Base: operating cash flow 13,461 19,968 23,223 26,436 29,434
Base: gross capex (19,000) (19,500) (20,000) (19,000) (18,500)
Base: FCF (OCF − gross capex) (5,539) 468 3,223 7,436 10,934
Base: capital offsets 5,500 3,000 1,500 1,000 800
Base: Intel's own "adjusted FCF" measure (39) 3,468 4,723 8,436 11,734
Bear: FCF (10,124) (4,857) (3,606) (2,038) (1,092)
Bull: FCF (1,734) 5,851 11,887 19,451 27,566

Three things not to miss. FY2026 free cash flow is roughly −$5.5bn in the base, and about −$13bn including the Apollo payment. Management guides "positive adjusted free cash flow for the full year" — but only "excluding the buyout of the Fab 34 joint investment," which consumed $7.7bn of cash plus $6.5bn of new debt. The capital offsets are running out: partner contributions went from $12,714M (FY2024) to $5,108M (FY2025), the Ireland SCIP has been bought back so Apollo contributes nothing further, and the $5.7bn of accelerated CHIPS money was received in 2025. And consensus capex is $2.4bn below the company's own guide — $15,239M against a guided ~$17.7bn gross and a Q1 2026 run-rate that annualizes to ~$19.9bn.

The interest-expense headwind arrives as the fabs finish. FY2025 reported interest expense was $1,091M, but Intel capitalized $1.2bn into fab construction, so gross interest incurred was $2,291M. As construction in progress is placed in service and capex moderates, the capitalizable base shrinks and reported interest rises toward gross even as debt falls. The base takes reported interest to $1,600M by FY2028–30 on a shrinking debt stack — and even that may be too low, because the entire premise is a shrinking capitalizable base.

17g. The NCI leak — the bear's most surprising result

Management guides non-controlling-interest income to roughly $1.1bn in each of 2027 and 2028, almost all of it Brookfield's Arizona SCIP.

Bear case FY2028E FY2030E FY2032E
Operating income $327M $1,791M $2,665M
less: NCI to Brookfield / Mobileye $(1,100)M $(1,200)M $(1,300)M
Net income attributable to Intel $(2,619)M $(1,556)M $(832)M
GAAP EPS $(0.48) $(0.28) $(0.15)

At bear-case profitability, the minority partners take more than the entire earnings of the company — even though operating income turns positive in FY2028. This is a structural feature of how Intel financed its fabs, and it is invisible in any analysis that stops at the operating line. (And with the depreciation correction above, the bear's operating income does not turn positive at all.)

17h. Sensitivity — the five drivers that matter

Swing in FY2030 operating income (base = $12,055M), one driver at a time.

Rank Driver Unit move OI impact Bear→bull swing
1 Consolidated gross margin ±1.0 pt ±$743M $8,921M
2 Intel Foundry external revenue ±$1,000M (at ~50% incremental) ±$500M $7,300M
3 Client unit share of the PC TAM ±1.0 pt (at ~50% incremental) ±$248M $5,035M
4 Server CPU ASP ±5% (at ~65% incremental) ±$698M $3,601M
5 Depreciation (CIP in-service timing) ±$1,000M ±$1,000M $2,600M

Drivers 1 and 2 overlap — external foundry revenue flows through gross margin — so they cannot be added. The incremental margins are computed, not assumed: the 65% on server ASP is the measured incremental product margin on price-led growth (Q1 2026: +$604M of product profit on +$926M of revenue), and the ~50% on external foundry revenue reflects capacity that is already built and already depreciating.

Driver 2 is the real binary, and it is the one the challenge above refuted on the downside. The base gives credit only to advanced packaging, where Intel has real differentiation and where the price is not set by a TSMC benchmark on a node Intel is behind on. The bull adds a 14A anchor customer landing on management's own dated promise. Even the bull's $17bn of external revenue in FY2030 falls short of the abandoned "#2 foundry by 2030" target of roughly $30bn — a target the CEO declined to reaffirm when asked directly.

17i. FY2026 specifically — the near-term testable claim

$M Q1 2026A Q2 2026E Q3 2026E Q4 2026E FY2026E
CCG 7,727 ~7,950 ~7,950 ~7,950 31,604
DCAI 5,052 ~5,600 ~5,850 ~6,100 22,386
All Other 628 ~630 ~650 ~670 2,578
Intel Foundry external 174 ~200 ~220 ~250 844
Total 13,577 ~14,380 ~14,670 ~14,970 ~57,236

CCG flat from Q2 is the CFO's own frame. The implied H2/H1 ratio of 1.06x is consistent with FY2025's actual 1.07x. Consensus's $62.4bn requires an H2/H1 of 1.24x — above Intel's decade maximum of 1.21x — in a year management guided the shape down to normal, guided the PC TAM down low double digits, and said H2 supply increases come "at a more measured pace than we anticipated 90 days ago."

The counter-argument, taken seriously: Intel has beaten its revenue guide six consecutive quarters by a widening margin, and the CEO says outright "my style is under promise, over delivering." Applying the six-quarter mean beat (+6.0%) to the Q2 midpoint gives about $15.2bn, above the top of the guided range. The base already assumes Q2 lands at about $14.4bn, above the midpoint — but not at the full beat, because the beats are being produced by supply arriving faster than management forecast, and management has now explicitly slowed the H2 supply ramp. If the beat pattern holds instead, FY2026 lands nearer $59–60bn and the base is about 4% light. That is the honest error bar on the nearest year, and it resolves on 2026-07-23.

17j. Implied incremental margins, tested against Intel's own history

Intel's best incremental margin on rising revenue in the last decade was 101.2% (FY2016→FY2017), with FY2017→FY2018 at 59.5% and FY2019→FY2020 at 24.5%.

Implied incremental margin, ex-restructuring FY2026E FY2027E FY2028E FY2030E FY2032E
Base 79.5% 51.5% 49.0% 50.2% 39.6%
Bull 75.3% 62.3% 60.4% 54.5% 47.7%

No year in any scenario exceeds Intel's historical best. The base settles at roughly 50%, which blends the measured 65% incremental margin on price-led growth against the roughly 0% on volume-led growth, plus a growing depreciation base that no revenue dollar absorbs. The figure to flag against the model is the FY2026 base incremental of 79.5%: it is high, and it is high for a defensible reason (FY2026 revenue growth is overwhelmingly price-led), but it exceeds Intel's realized FY2018 and FY2020 figures, and it is the first line to break if the FY2026 ASP gains prove less durable within the year than the Q1 exit rate implies.
