The base is the only one of the four paths that violates no base-rate constraint. The bull breaches two and consensus breaches two — including the one that has never happened in 30 years of large US semiconductor history: nobody has delivered top-quintile growth and a mid-twenties operating margin simultaneously, three years out from a loss year. That does not make the bull impossible. It makes it an outcome at or beyond the maximum of the historical distribution, which is what a bull case should be and is not what a consensus should be.

17l. Declared model limits

  1. The escrowed-shares derivative is set to zero in all three scenarios. It is share-settled and marked through interest and other, net: a rising Intel share price mechanically produces P&L losses ($1,796M in FY2025; a further $1.1bn in Q1 2026 alone). It has negative convexity and it is growing. Every GAAP EPS line in this model is overstated in any scenario where the stock appreciates — and it appreciates most in the bull.
  2. The 241M-share U.S. government warrant ($20.00 strike) is excluded from all scenarios. It triggers precisely in the bull. The bull's FY2030 EPS of $4.20 is therefore overstated by up to about 4.5% on the warrant alone, before the roughly 150M of remaining escrowed shares.
  3. The 14A "pause or discontinue" scenario is not modelled. It is a discrete event, not a driver delta, so it cannot be expressed in the bear case; the bear instead assumes Intel keeps spending and keeps missing. Hold it as a separate, un-priced tail.
  4. A Brookfield/Arizona SCIP buyout would be a roughly $14.5bn cash call on the Ireland precedent. Nothing obliges Intel to do it; Intel has now demonstrated that it will. Not modelled.
  5. The split of Intel Foundry's $17,519M intersegment revenue between CCG and DCAI is not disclosed, so no economic segment margin exists for either product segment. Every segment margin in the projections is a reported-basis figure.
  6. Absolute unit volumes are never disclosed in any period. The unit base is triangulated; the ASP changes are anchored.

18. Risks

Gap flagged at the top of this section, per §20: China is 24.0% of FY2025 revenue ($12,694M, down 18.3% from $15,532M) and does not appear in the risk list below. The risk inventory covers Israel, Taiwan and ASML as supply-side single points of failure but never sizes the demand-side exposure to Chinese state-procurement exclusion, domestic x86 substitution (Hygon, Zhaoxin, Loongson) or further export-control tightening. The second-largest billing region is in structural decline and is not sized below (§20).

Intel cut the FY2025 10-K's risk-factor section from 36 headings to 26 and from 115k to 105k characters while adding the two most severe risks in the filing's history. It also deleted the standalone "We have ceased to return capital to stockholders" factor while the underlying fact persists (FY2025 dividends and buybacks were both zero), and deleted the corporate-responsibility factor entirely. The Q1 2026 10-Q added no new or amended risk factors, in a quarter that included a $3.9bn goodwill impairment and a $14.2bn subsequent-event buyout.

R1 — The Intel 14A gate: leading-edge discontinuation (existential)

Mechanism: Intel 14A is the first node designed from inception for external customers, and it requires an anchor customer to cover the fixed cost. Absent one, Intel says it may pause or discontinue 14A and all successor leading-edge nodes, becoming permanently dependent on TSMC for its own high-end products — with no long-term contract in place. Exposure: More than $100bn of net PP&E, "the substantial majority of which we estimate relate to our foundry business." Government incentive clawback (Intel received $5.7bn of accelerated CHIPS disbursements). SCIP penalty payments. Intel calls the decision "effectively irreversible." Leading indicator, dated: The CFO on the Q4 2025 call: customers' window to secure 14A capacity "will be in the back half of this year" — so the gate resolves in 2H 2026. Watch the 0.9 PDK release (0.5 shipped in Q1 2026), any named 14A customer, Ohio construction pace, and 14A risk production guided to "the later part of 2027." Mitigation, double-edged: Intel is withholding 14A capacity capex until a customer signs, which protects cash but guarantees it cannot promise near-term capacity to win the customer. That is a circularity, not a mitigation. Separately, the Q1 2026 10-Q softened the test to include Intel's own product roadmap, and Intel has moved more of its own tiles onto 14A. The 10-K also states that while Intel's plan includes internal 14A products, it is "maintaining the option" to have post-18A products "produced internally or by an external foundry." Intel has not foreclosed using someone else's fab for its own next-generation parts.

R2 — Intel Foundry's structural loss and the depreciation wall (severe)

Mechanism: Intel Foundry absorbs leading-edge R&D and the full Intel 18A early-ramp cost. Its revenue is 98% intersegment, so its loss is a real consolidated GAAP and cash loss, not a transfer artifact. Exposure: FY2025 operating loss $10,318M on $17,826M of segment revenue, after $950M of impairments and accelerated depreciation. Q1 2026 loss $2,437M with $174M of external revenue. Consolidated FY2025 operating result: a $2,214M loss despite $12,739M of Intel Products operating income. D&A was $10,757M and is still climbing: 2026 capex is guided flat but tool spend is up ~25%, and tools depreciate faster than buildings. $34,543M of construction in progress is not yet depreciating. Leading indicator: The quarterly Intel Foundry operating loss and external revenue; the D&A line; quarterly impairment and accelerated-depreciation charges ($950M in FY2025 against $3.3bn in FY2024). Mitigation: Cost cuts (R&D down from $16,546M to $13,774M) and 18A yields running ahead of internal plan. But the CFO still calls 18A "a pretty decent headwind to our gross margins" and says foundry-average gross margin is "multiple, multiple quarters" away.

R3 — Price-led revenue masking volume and share erosion (severe, and under-appreciated)

Mechanism: Q1 2026's celebrated print was entirely ASP and mix. Units declined in both product segments. Intel is harvesting price under a supply constraint while its competitor takes units. Exposure:

Q1 2026 vs Q1 2025 ASP Volume Revenue
Client (notebook + desktop) +16% (13)% $6.6bn, +$54M
Server +27% (5)% +$696M

In the same quarter, AMD's Data Center revenue of $5,775M (+57% y/y) exceeded Intel DCAI's $5,052M (+22%). (Caveat: AMD's Data Center segment bundles Instinct GPUs and FPGAs, so this is not a like-for-like server-CPU comparison — but the growth gap and Intel's −5% server volume are like-for-like directional facts.) Leading indicator: The volume-percentage lines in each 10-Q's CCG and DCAI MD&A; Mercury Research unit share; AMD's Data Center segment revenue. Mitigation: Xeon 6, the Google multi-year LTA, and the Granite/Diamond/Coral Rapids roadmap. Note that Coral Rapids is where Intel finally adds simultaneous multithreading "so we can compete effectively with AMD" — which is an admission that the current server part is architecturally behind.

R4 — Input-cost squeeze (memory, substrates, T-glass) into a declining PC TAM (high)

Mechanism: DRAM/NAND, advanced substrates and T-glass prices are rising on AI demand. Intel is passing them through with demand-based pricing actions — into a PC market management itself says is shrinking. Exposure: The CFO: "the one cautionary concern I have on gross margin in the back half of the year is just some of the materials have gone up... substrates are going up, T glass. We've got memory going up." Q2 2026 gross margin guided down to 39% from 41% actual, despite an improving DCAI mix. The FY2025 10-K names "current industry supply constraints for memory chips, substrates and foundry capacity." The elasticity trap: management guides the PC industry down double digits in units in 2026 while saying Intel will be less affected "partly because of pricing a little bit, but also because of inventory replenishment at the customer level." Channel replenishment is a pull-forward that reverses, and pricing into a double-digit-declining TAM invites share loss. Client revenue is guided flat from Q2 onward. Leading indicator: Sequential gross margin against the 39% guide; the client volume line; distributor and OEM inventory commentary; DRAM contract pricing.

R5 — Liquidity and re-levering around the $14.2bn Apollo buyout (high)

Mechanism: Intel bought out Apollo's 49% of Ireland SCIP to remove the NCI drag and the liquidated-damages derivative, but paid cash it does not currently generate. Exposure: ~$14.2bn cash consideration against cash plus short-term investments of $32,789M at Q1 2026 (down $4.6bn in one quarter), total debt of $45,031M, and Q1 2026 operating cash flow of $1.1bn against $5.0bn of gross capex. Funded with ~$7.7bn of cash plus a ~$6.5bn term loan, taking debt toward ~$51.5bn. Leading indicator: Cash and short-term investments; adjusted free cash flow; commercial-paper usage; the 364-day facility, which was cut from $5.0bn to a three-year $3.0bn; and credit-rating actions — the FY2025 10-K explicitly flags "the risk of a future downgrade in our credit ratings." Mitigation: A $7.0bn revolver undrawn to February 2029, an open shelf registration, and $7.0bn of strategic equity already banked. No dividend and no buyback to cut — that lever is already pulled.

R6 — Customer concentration (high)

Mechanism: Three PC OEMs are nearly half the company, and the growth segment's customers are simultaneously building the silicon that replaces Intel's. Exposure: Three largest customers = 43% of FY2025 net revenue (45% FY2024, 40% FY2023): Dell 19%, Lenovo 12%, HP Inc. 12% per the XBRL major-customer tags (the narrative anonymizes them as Customer A/B/C). "Substantially all" from Intel Products. Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta are named as customers and as competitors building their own silicon. What a defection costs is not sized here. Apple's 2020 exit is the live precedent and is not quantified, and Dell's and HP's own filings carry the Intel-versus-AMD-versus-Qualcomm sourcing commentary that would size it (§20). Leading indicator: The concentration percentages in each 10-K; hyperscaler in-house silicon announcements; Dell/HP/Lenovo AMD-based SKU mix. Mitigation: The Google multi-year LTA and Xeon 6 as host CPU for NVIDIA's DGX Rubin NVL8 convert two threats into contracted demand. Real, but small against 43%.

R7 — The U.S. government as a large shareholder (high, and novel)

Mechanism: In Q3 2025 the Department of Commerce took 275M shares, a warrant for 241M shares at $20.00 (exercisable if Intel ceases to own ≥51% of Intel Foundry), and 159M escrowed shares. Exposure: (a) Dilution: shares outstanding went 4,330M → 4,994M in FY2025, and the warrant is a further ~241M-share overhang triggered precisely by the foundry separation many bulls want. (b) Retaliation: sales outside the U.S. were 70% of 2025 revenue, with China at 24%, and Intel warns the U.S. stake "could subject us to additional regulations, obligations or restrictions, such as foreign subsidy laws." (c) Legal: Intel concedes branches of the U.S. government "could determine in the future that all or a portion of the transactions were unauthorized, void or voidable," and that "enforcement against a government counterparty is inherently uncertain." (d) Grant access: converting grants to equity "may cause other government entities to seek to convert their existing grant arrangements... into equity investments or be unwilling to support us with future grants." Accounting caveat: the accounting was changed after an SEC staff consultation that concluded in Q4 2025, after the Q3 2025 10-Q was filed. Any figure on this topic taken from that 10-Q is stale. Leading indicator: Foundry-separation news (which arms the warrant); EU or China foreign-subsidy proceedings. An open commercial question: whether a foundry whose largest shareholder is the U.S. government is a better or worse counterparty for Chinese, Korean and Taiwanese fabless customers, and for Apple, Qualcomm and NVIDIA weighing supply-chain politics. The stake is analyzed only as dilution, never as a commercial variable — and the 14A decision turns on that.

R8 — Single points of failure: Israel, Taiwan/TSMC, ASML (high tail)

Israel: the FY2025 10-K states: "a significant portion of our revenues are generated from products using our Intel 7 node that are manufactured at our fabrication facility in Israel" and "we are not insured for business interruptions resulting from war or political violence." Intel 7 was the majority of internal processor production by revenue in 2025 and is expected to be almost half in 2026. Israeli PP&E is self-insured, and Mobileye is also headquartered there. This is the largest uninsured single-site exposure in the filing. TSMC / Taiwan: Intel's disaggregated tiles depend on TSMC; "We have no long-term contract with TSMC"; "There are few foundries capable of producing the leading-edge and near-leading-edge nodes needed for our products — currently only TSMC and Samsung." Its primary foundry competitor is also a critical supplier. ASML: named sole supplier of the EUV tools for Intel 4, Intel 3 and Intel 18A, and of the high-NA tools contemplated for 14A. Leading indicator: Israel/Iran escalation; the Taiwan Strait; ASML high-NA shipment slots; the Intel 7 share-of-production disclosure in each 10-K.

R9 — Goodwill and the acquisition record (medium-high)

Exposure: Q1 2026: a $3.9bn non-cash goodwill impairment, substantially all Mobileye, driven by "the sustained decline in Mobileye's market capitalization" and booked to corporate unallocated. FY2024 goodwill impairment was $2,984M. Goodwill remaining: $23,912M. Gaudi was written off in stages: $375M (2025) plus $922M (2024) of inventory charges, with the 10-K conceding it "was unsuccessful." Leading indicator: Mobileye's market capitalization against its carrying value; the quarterly qualitative goodwill-trigger language.

R10 — Degrading disclosure granularity (medium, but it amplifies everything above)

Risk-factor headings 36 → 26; the capital-return and ESG factors deleted; segment gross margin no longer disclosed (the FY2024 10-K gave DCAI 47% and 49%); no segment assets, no segment depreciation, no segment balance sheet; absolute unit volumes never given; 18A yield described by the CFO as "a closely guarded proprietary piece of information"; the advanced-packaging backlog sized only verbally; and a new unreconciled management metric ("AI-driven businesses = 60% of revenue, +40% y/y") introduced in Q1 2026 and tied to no segment. It matters because segment ROIC and segment EBITDA cannot be derived, Intel Products' 29–33% margins cannot be tested, and the foundry turn cannot be independently verified.

The bad-quarter scenario — these do not fire independently

The realistic 2H 2026 downside is a single joint event. The PC TAM declines double digits and the Q1 channel replenishment reverses, so client volume worsens beyond −13%. Memory, substrate and T-glass costs keep rising, so the 39% Q2 gross-margin guide is missed and further pricing actions accelerate the unit-share loss to AMD. Panther Lake volume rises six- or seven-fold sequentially on Intel 18A, still below corporate-average margin, so mix drags gross margin as the cost squeeze bites. The 2H 2026 14A customer window closes with no signature, moving the pause-or-discontinue clause from disclosure to decision and arming impairments against $100bn-plus of PP&E, government clawbacks and SCIP penalties. And all of it lands on a balance sheet that just spent $14.2bn on the Apollo buyout with negative free cash flow. The common trigger is gross margin: it is the single line that expresses the PC TAM, the input costs, the 18A mix and the foundry ramp at once.

19. Source disclosure

Local databases and archives used: the primary sources are the archived filings at archive\INTC\ — ten 10-Ks (FY2016–FY2025), four 10-Qs (2025 Q1–Q3, 2026 Q1), 48 earnings-call transcripts (Q2 2014 – Q1 2026), presentation transcripts (2015–2025), and 19 investor decks (2015-08-27 to 2026-04-23, 1,395 slides rendered). Peer filings were bootstrapped for AMD, NVDA, QCOM, AVGO, MU, DELL, HPQ and MBLY. SEC XBRL companyfacts (CIK 0000050863) supplied the three-statement history. Bloomberg (live terminal, pulled 2026-07-11) supplied prices, total returns, price-to-book, EV/EBITDA, BEst consensus, ratings, target prices and the peer comp panel. Intel's proxy statements (2018–2026) supplied the compensation record.

Series built for this company: a ten-year annual financial history (FY2016–FY2025), a thirteen-quarter series, three forward scenarios, 29 model assumptions, a 29-row comparable-company table, 23 guide-to-actual pairs, and a base-rate panel of 37 tickers, 1996–2026.

Gaps and failures:

  • Firecrawl was unavailable (HTTP 402, out of credits), so web collection fell back to built-in search. The three industry trackers this company most needs — Mercury Research, IDC and TrendForce — stayed paywalled and were reached only through trade-press renderings, which disagreed with each other in two places (AMD client unit share 29.6% versus 30.0%, depending on whether embedded SoCs are included; ARM's server share 13.2% versus 17.7%, depending on the denominator). The share data underneath §4 and §6 is therefore second-hand throughout.
  • 10K-redlines has no Intel coverage, so the year-over-year risk-factor diffs the routing table points to do not exist. They were rebuilt by hand from the archived Item 1A texts for FY2019–FY2025. Not a blocker.
  • The routed guidance store was empty (a broken CLI configuration killed the extraction step), and the analysis profile written for Intel is a mis-seeded copy of Applied Materials'. The guidance scorecard was rebuilt from the 23 archived 8-K earnings releases and the transcripts.
  • Bloomberg credit ratings and bond yields were never pulled, even though the terminal was live all run. The August 2025 downgrade agency is therefore unnamed, Moody's and Fitch positions are unknown, and §12's weighted-average cost of debt is computed from 10-K coupons. This is the most consequential omission, because market yields are the one input that could falsify the refinancing conclusion for roughly $51bn of debt, a fresh $6.5bn raise and a 2027 maturity wall.
  • Form 4 insider transactions were never pulled, although EDGAR serves them free, so open-market insider buying and selling outside the CEO's contractual $25M purchase is unverified.
  • No sell-side bear case exists locally. The OC-Sellside digest holds exactly one Intel-covering report of 40, and it is bullish (BofA, 2026-06-23). A claimed cluster of June 2026 downgrades was found only on low-quality content-farm sources and could not be corroborated from Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC or Barron's; it is excluded and should not be relied upon.
  • Two decks central to the foundry thesis are missing from the archive: Intel Accelerated (July 2021, the node roadmap event) and Foundry Direct Connect (2024, the foundry customer event). The 2025 Direct Connect transcript is present; the decks are not.
  • No external dataset was pulled. The registry surfaced exactly one for the semiconductor archetype (memory spot pricing, a paid web mosaic) and it was not fetched. See Appendix C.
  • Peer filings unavailable locally: TSMC, GlobalFoundries, UMC, SMIC and Samsung are foreign private issuers or non-US filers, so all of their financials here are from company results releases and TrendForce rankings, tagged [web].
  • Survivorship bias in the base-rate panel: a Bloomberg ticker panel contains only surviving companies. Freescale, Xilinx, Altera, IDT, Cypress, Toshiba memory, Elpida and Qimonda are absent. Every recovery base rate quoted is therefore biased upward.

Discrepancy log summary: twelve source disagreements were logged and resolved. The material ones: Intel restated FY2016–FY2017 gross profit and operating income when it adopted ASU 2017-07 (the recast figures are used throughout, so the ten-year margin series is on one basis); Bloomberg reports the pre-restatement FY2021 operating cash flow ($29,991M, not $29,456M) and a gross capex $1,596M above the filing in FY2021, so the filings win in both cases; Intel's FY2019 operating cash flow is stated two different ways in its own filings ($33,145M in the cash-flow statement, $32,618M in a later MD&A table) and is unresolved; and two invested-capital definitions are in play, producing a FY2025 figure of $135,529M (cash and short-term investments netted) versus $159,071M (cash only). The tighter definition is used in §3 and the wider one in §14c, and both are stated where they appear.

Web sources: 41 web citations were used across the run, drawn from roughly 25 domains. The heaviest use is trade press rendering paywalled research: theregister.com, tomshardware.com, hothardware.com, wccftech.com (Mercury Research share data); idc.com and gartner.com (PC shipments); trendforce.com (foundry share, CoWoS capacity, DRAM pricing); investor.tsmc.com, asml.com, ir.amd.com, nvidianews.nvidia.com (peer financials); spectrum.ieee.org and semianalysis.com (process technology); and stockanalysis.com, tradingkey.com (market data). Every material web claim is quoted in Appendix B.

Claims flagged [web, unverified]: none. Every web source cited for a material claim was re-fetched successfully during verification, and two were contradicted by their own source and have been corrected in the body: the claim that Intel 18A trails TSMC N2 on both published density metrics (IEEE Spectrum reports the two as tied on SRAM), and the claim that TSMC adopts high-NA EUV from its A14 node in 2028 (TrendForce reports that TSMC has decided not to adopt high-NA for its 1.4nm node).

Estimates by method: 34 [estimate: …] figures appear above. By method: 11 use third-party unit share × a disclosed revenue line (Intel's client and server unit counts, ASPs, and the derived share series); 7 on pro-rata allocation of a disclosed segment loss (the fully-loaded CCG and DCAI margins); 5 on bottom-up physical arithmetic (wafer counts, die sizes, bill-of-materials stacks); 4 on residual arithmetic from consensus (the implied Intel Foundry operating income, the implied DCAI path, the implied consensus share count); 3 on peer-multiple or precedent application (the Brookfield unwind cost, the Apollo IRR, the IMS implied valuation); and 4 on inverted disclosure (the effective floating-rate exposure, the FY2025 Intel Foundry gross margin and opex, the segment-cost reconstructions). Every estimate is quoted with its bounds; none is presented as a point figure.

One correction worth carrying: on the public-comp performance ranking, Intel does not lead the universe except Micron — UMC leads it year-to-date and Samsung over one year. Two of the 29 model assumptions are refuted (Intel Foundry external revenue and the depreciation scenario structure) and are flagged in §17 wherever the output depends on them; a further 17 were judged weak and are marked in the assumptions table.

External datasets: one is available for this company's archetype and none was pulled. See Appendix C.

20. What we still don't know / monitoring KPIs

Material gaps

  1. "All Other" is covered as accounting, never as a business. Mobileye is $1,900M of revenue and an 80%-owned listed stake Intel could monetize against the unquantified Arizona SCIP exit. No unit volumes, no design-win pipeline, no competitive position against NVIDIA DRIVE or Qualcomm Snapdragon Ride, and nothing establishing why the $3.9bn Q1 2026 goodwill impairment happened or whether the remaining carrying value is at further risk. Flagged at the top of §1.
  2. IMS Nanofabrication is entirely unanalyzed — no revenue, growth, margin or current mark — even though it is a near-monopoly in multi-beam mask writing in which Bain and TSMC bought minority stakes in 2023, and it is the one acquisition in Intel's ledger that visibly compounded. §11's judgment on Intel as an acquirer is therefore graded only on the failures.
  3. Advanced packaging is not sized. No EMIB/Foveros capacity in wafers per month, no ASP, no share estimate against TSMC's CoWoS, no backlog in dollars, no named customer. It is treated throughout as a feature of Intel Foundry, not as its own economic unit — yet it is the only credible external-revenue path in the company and the one §17's foundry ramp assumes. This is the most important undisclosed number at Intel.
  4. China at 24% of revenue has no risk entry. Flagged at the top of §18.
  5. What Intel Products would earn buying wafers at merchant prices is unknown. CCG's and DCAI's margins are transfer-price constructs and the Intel Foundry loss allocation is banded at 55–70%, so there is no basis on which CCG and DCAI can be compared like-for-like to AMD, NVIDIA or Qualcomm. Every input needed to construct one (TSMC wafer pricing, Intel die sizes, the $17,519M intersegment line) exists. Flagged at the top of §3.
  6. Bloomberg credit ratings and bond yields were not pulled, so the cost of debt in §12 is a coupon calculation, not a market one, and the August 2025 downgrade agency is unnamed.
  7. Form 4 insider transactions were not pulled, so §10's alignment analysis has a blank at the moment the stock rose roughly 270% and executive pay is heavily equity-linked.
  8. The Arizona SCIP exit terms were never checked against the counterparty. Intel's filings disclose no put, no call and no formula. Brookfield Infrastructure files with the SEC and holds earnings calls that may describe the terms, which would put a number on a $14bn-plus exposure.
  9. Pre-FY2016 filings are absent from the archive, so the McAfee purchase-price allocation and the price paid for IMS cannot be read from any filing, and the 14nm/10nm capital decisions of 2013–2015 that originated the whole story have no primary source in the file.
  10. FY2023 quarterly segment data does not exist on the current basis (the Q1 2025 recast restated the FY2024 quarters but never FY2023), so the "DCAI is inflecting" claim — the central bull point — is year-over-year comparable for only five quarters.
  11. The 21% one-week drawdown to 2026-07-09 on 18A-yield press reporting is logged but never reconciled against management's "yields ahead of plan" claim. The front-matter market table, §15 and §7's ranking all use a price that moved on an unadjudicated claim.
  12. Q2 2026 prints on 2026-07-23, so the analysis is anchored on Q1 2026 data that is eleven weeks old, with only the live Q2 guide as a forward point. The DCAI-inflection and supply-constraint conclusions will be re-based within two weeks of publication.

Open questions

  • What is the actual internal transfer price Intel Foundry charges Intel Products, per wafer or as a markup? It determines the entire product-versus-foundry profit split and is never disclosed. A change in the methodology alone could move roughly $10bn between the two segments without any change in economics.
  • How much of the $10,757M of FY2025 depreciation is in Intel Foundry? Intel says "the substantial majority" and refuses to be more precise.
  • What is the split of Intel Foundry's $174M of Q1 2026 external revenue between Altera (a 49%-owned related party still buying wafers), the U.S. government (Secure Enclave), and arm's-length third-party customers? This single disclosure would settle whether a merchant foundry business exists at all.
  • What is Intel 18A's actual defect density? Never disclosed, at any point, in any filing or call. Every yield claim is therefore an adjective, and "ahead of plan" is unfalsifiable because the plan is not disclosed either.
  • Why is Intel 7 — a node in volume since 2017 — the binding constraint, and what does relieving it cost and take? How much Intel 7 capacity exists, how much was converted to Intel 4/3/18A (which would make the shortage partly self-inflicted), what it costs and how long it takes to add mature-node capacity back, and how much revenue was actually foregone. "Starts with a B" is the only bound available.
  • What share of Intel's product revenue is manufactured by TSMC? Not disclosed. It is the single cleanest measure of whether the integrated model is working.
  • What is the forward tax rate, and what happens to the $9,900M deferred-tax valuation allowance on a recovery? The model includes a tax line and an EPS line, and the assumption file contains a tax rate whose stated mechanism is backwards (a valuation allowance does not suppress a running book rate; its release is a one-time benefit). A release versus no release moves the EPS ladder materially.
  • Does the ~2027 Intel Foundry breakeven target still stand as a company commitment, or has it become an IR talking point? It has been absent from prepared remarks for six quarters. The promised 2026 investor day — the first since February 2022 — will settle it, and will also show whether Intel ever reconciles the 2022 model to what happened.
  • What does an OEM defection actually cost? Dell, HP and Lenovo are 43% of revenue and all three are PC makers. Apple's 2020 exit is the live precedent and is nowhere sized.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights & key slides

Nineteen decks are archived, spanning 2015-08-27 to 2026-04-23 (1,395 slides). The decks are the only place where Intel's forward financial models are stated in numbers and then left standing to be marked to market. The 10-K never restates an abandoned target; the decks do. What follows is the consolidated digest of the additive insights, each cross-referenced to the body section it also informs.

  • The say/do ledger is the archive's core contribution, and it is not reconstructible from the filings. Laying the 2015, 2017, 2019, 2022 and 2024 models side by side against what was delivered gives a clean record: FY2016 gross margin "~62% ±2pts" (delivered 60.9%); a 2017 three-year model in which gross margin "declines modestly, remains in the top half of the historical range" (it reached 32.7%); a 2019 model with FY2019 revenue of $76–78bn (delivered $72.0bn) and gross margin bottoming in 2021 (it kept declining to 2024); and the February 2022 long-term model, every line of which was missed by a wide margin. [deck: Investor Meeting 2022, 2022-02-17, slides 35, 61, 62] → §14.
  • Intel published, in its own hand, the process lead/lag scorecard that documents the collapse. [deck: Internal Foundry Model webinar, 2023-06-21, slide 10] rates Intel's own nodes against the competition: 32nm "++", 22nm "++", 14nm "+", 10nm "− −", Intel 4 "−", Intel 3 "−", Intel 20A "−", Intel 18A "+". Management is admitting it went from a two-notch lead at 22nm to a two-notch deficit at 10nm and stayed behind for four consecutive nodes. This is the cleanest statement of the competitive collapse in the corpus, and it appears only in the deck. → §2, §3.
  • "The EUV Wall" is the most important economic slide in the decks. [deck: New Segment Reporting webinar, 2024-04-02, slide 16] gives Intel's own economics of a leading-edge fab: pre-EUV wafers, ~$12.5bn capex per fab and ~0% margin per wafer start, five players; EUV, ~$25bn and ~40%, two to three players; high-NA, $25–30bn and ~50%, ~2 players. Management is stating that pre-EUV wafers earn approximately zero margin — which is why Intel Foundry loses money while the majority of its output is Intel 7 — and that the industry supports only about two leading-edge players at high-NA. → §1c, §4c, §17.
  • Intel quantified its own margin penalty for being an integrated device manufacturer, and it is the most damaging chart the company has ever published about itself. [deck: Internal Foundry Model webinar, 2023-06-21, slide 14, sourced by Intel to a Bain study] plots a "synthetic IDM" — the gross margin a company would earn combining a fabless designer's margin with a merchant foundry's — against Intel's own GAAP gross margin, 2015–2022. The two lines cross in 2017. By 2022 the synthetic IDM is at roughly 70% and Intel at roughly 43%: a more than 20-point gross-margin penalty for vertical integration. → §3, §5.
  • The internal-foundry transfer-pricing model is explained with a worked P&L, and it licenses the caveat this entire dossier depends on. [deck: Internal Foundry Model webinar, 2023-06-21, slide 12]: under IDM 2.0 the manufacturing arm bills the business unit $110 for $100 of cost, so manufacturing shows a 9% gross margin and a −18% operating margin by construction while the business unit shows 45% and 20%. This is management's own worked example of why CCG's 29% and DCAI's 20% are not economic margins and why Intel Foundry's −58% is not an external-market loss. → §1, §3, §7.
  • The foundry margin bridge is fully specified, so it can be tested. [deck: New Segment Reporting webinar, 2024-04-02, slides 28–32] decomposes Intel Foundry's path from a −37% operating margin to breakeven into four named levers with point ranges (transistor leadership 9–11 pts, internal mix and scale 7–9 pts, capital and cost efficiency 12–14 pts, opex leverage 5–7 pts), and gives node-level gross margins: pre-EUV ~20%, advanced packaging 30–40%, EUV nodes 40–50%. Every foundry forecast should be built off these levers and tested against the FY2025 actual of −58%. → §17.
  • Foundry attempt #1 is in the archive and nowhere else. [deck: Technology & Manufacturing Day, 2017-03-28, slides 25–31] launched "Intel Custom Foundry" with a 22FFL platform, 14nm and 10nm offerings, EMIB, and the statement "we are building a foundry franchise." It was closed in 2018. Any assessment of management's credibility on Intel Foundry has to start from the fact that this is the second attempt, not the first. → §3, §14.
  • The 2017 deck states the engineering bet that broke the company, by name and with numbers, before it broke. [deck: Technology & Manufacturing Day, 2017-03-28, slides 11, 12, 17] promised "hyper scaling" — 0.43x die-area scaling on 10nm versus the 0.62x achieved on 45nm and 32nm — and claimed Intel's 14nm was "~3 years ahead." The 10nm hyper-scaling target (cobalt interconnect, contact-over-active-gate and self-aligned quad patterning, all at once, without EUV) is precisely what did not yield. The 10-K describes the delay as an outcome; the deck shows the bet. → §2, §9.
  • The AI story was told three times and mutated each time. 2016 AI Day: Nervana, with a claimed 100x reduction in time-to-train by 2020 and the closing slide "Why Intel Wins in AI." 2017 Investor Day: 97% of AI servers ran on Intel architecture — management treated that as ownership; it was the peak. 2023 DCAI webinar: Gaudi 2 → Gaudi 3 → Falcon Shores. 2026 Q1 earnings: "Intel CPUs Foundational to Inference and Agentic — CPU-to-Accelerator ratio narrowing." Intel has stopped claiming the accelerator socket and now claims the host-CPU socket beside someone else's accelerator. → §2, §6.
  • CCG's historical pricing power is documented, and it is the benchmark against which today's flat ASPs should be judged. [deck: Investor Meeting 2019, 2019-05-08, slides 83, 85]: the PC TAM declined roughly 30% from 377M units (2011) to 272M (2016), yet CCG's revenue and operating income grew from $32.2bn/$8.2bn (2015) to $37bn/$14.2bn (2018). CCG's operating income nearly doubled on a shrinking TAM, through mix and sell-up. → §1, §4a.
  • The buyback policy contradicts itself on the same slide. [deck: Investor Meeting 2019, 2019-05-08, slides 116, 117] states "be opportunistic on buybacks" and, on the facing slide, shows the largest buyback in the series ($10.7bn) in 2018, the year the stock made its cycle high. → §10.
  • Intel disclosed hard internal-efficiency metrics at the point of the reorganization, and has never reported against them since. [deck: New Segment Reporting webinar, 2024-04-02, slide 30]: production expedites down 95%; a 5–10% reduction in capex to deliver the same volume; next-generation client test time reduced 75%; a 10–15% wafer-cost improvement from a faster move from technology development to high-volume manufacturing. These are the only quantified internal-efficiency metrics Intel has published, and they are the leading indicators for whether the foundry cost lever is real. → §17, §20.

Contradictions across the deck archive: Intel's 2017 claim of a three-year 14nm lead against its own 2023 "− −" rating of 10nm. Capital intensity presented as a controlled dial at 20% of revenue in 2017, reaching roughly 40% by 2022 on Intel's own chart. "Opportunistic" buybacks executed at the cycle high. ">$15B of lifetime deal value and a clear path to >$15B annual external revenue by 2030" (April 2024) against the FY2025 10-K's "unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of our nodes" and $307M of actual external revenue. And Gelsinger's "say/do ratio is high," asserted on the April 2024 deck, falsified by the 2022 long-term model published by the same management two years earlier.

Key-slide gallery: thirty slides were curated to the archive key-slide set, ordered chronologically from the 2015 Data Center Day to the Q1 2026 earnings deck. They are rendered from archive\INTC\decks\key_slides\captions.json.

Appendix C — External data sources

The registry identified one external dataset relevant to Intel's archetype (semiconductor). The deep dive does not auto-fetch external data; what follows is a menu, not fetched data. No figures below are drawn from the source, and none is fabricated.

memory_spot_pricing — DRAM/NAND spot and contract pricing (mosaic)
What it is A partial, assembled series of DRAM and NAND spot and contract price points, built from scattered dated citations. The primary source (TrendForce) is paid, so the series would be a web mosaic, not a comprehensive dataset.
What it measures The direction and magnitude of memory price changes over time: PC DRAM contract price trend, NAND price trend, and the server DRAM curve.
How it could inform this company Memory is the single named driver of Intel's 2H 2026 gross-margin risk. The CFO has flagged DRAM and HBM input costs as a growing headwind, the FY2025 10-K names "industry supply constraints for memory chips," and IDC's −11.3% PC unit forecast for 2026 is driven by memory-led system price inflation. A dated memory price series would test two things currently taken on management's word and on trade-press figures: whether the input-cost squeeze in §5 and R4 is intensifying or easing, and whether the PC unit destruction in §6 has further to run. It would strengthen §6 (secular trends) and the operational-KPI subsection of §13.
Cadence Irregular — the mosaic would be assembled from dated points, with coverage gaps stated explicitly.
Confidence if pulled Medium to low, with bounds. Mosaic findings are never presented as comprehensive.
Status Not pulled.

No other external dataset in the registry matches Intel. Several free and credible series that would strengthen this analysis are absent from the registry: WSTS/SIA billings, IDC's PC shipment releases, Census semiconductor shipment data, and the CHIPS disbursement records. Their absence is noted in §20.
